# OpenHikes repository instructions

## Build and test

The main project requires Xcode 27+, the iOS 27.0 platform (the trail maker's route list reorders with iOS 27's `reorderable()`), and a development team capable of signing the WeatherKit entitlement, the shared App Group, the iCloud container, the push and Time Sensitive Notifications entitlements and HealthKit. The shared package can be built and tested independently on macOS.

```sh
# Boot the simulator first. Anything below that runs tests needs this.
xcrun simctl boot "iPhone 18 Pro" || true
xcrun simctl bootstatus "iPhone 18 Pro" -b

# Build the app, its embedded widget and the watch app. The watch target is a
# dependency of the app, so this compiles it for watchOS too.
xcodebuild build \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 18 Pro'

# The watch app alone, which is the faster loop while working on it. There is
# no watch test bundle — see "The watch app" below for why, and for where the
# testable half of it lives instead.
xcodebuild build \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikesWatch \
  -destination 'generic/platform=watchOS Simulator'

# Run the two app-hosted unit bundles: the default local gate, ~20 seconds
xcodebuild test \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 18 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests -only-testing:OpenWidgetTests

# Run everything the scheme's plan carries, UI automation included: ~13 minutes.
# This is not "the unit tests with extra safety" — OpenHikes.xctestplan lists
# OpenHikesUITests too, and omitting -only-testing: is the whole difference
# between a twenty-second gate and a quarter-hour one.
xcodebuild test \
  -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj \
  -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 18 Pro'

# Run one app test suite or one test method
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 18 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests/HikeStatisticsTests
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 18 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenHikesTests/HikeStatisticsTests/elevationGainAndLoss\(\)

# Run just the widget bundle
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 18 Pro' \
  -only-testing:OpenWidgetTests

# Run simulator UI automation and launch performance metrics
xcodebuild test -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikesUI \
  -destination 'platform=iOS Simulator,name=iPhone 18 Pro'

# Run the standalone shared-package suite
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared

# Run one shared-package suite or test
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared --filter MercatorTests
swift test --package-path OpenHikesShared \
  --filter 'OpenHikesSharedTests.MercatorTests/tileIndicesUnchanged'

# The shell scripts, against stubbed xcrun/xcodebuild/swiftlint/periphery
Scripts/run-script-tests.sh
```

Boot the simulator before running any of the test commands, and treat that as part of the command rather than a refinement of it. A cold simulator is a known source of *"Early unexpected exit, operation never finished bootstrapping"*: the host app is killed by the watchdog that is timing its launch, and the run fails without a single test having reported anything. CI boots as its own step in both the `unit-tests` and `accessibility-ui-tests` jobs for exactly this reason, and the failure is not confined to a shared runner — the documented command run as written against a cold simulator on `main` took 342 seconds to fail with *"The test runner hung before establishing connection"*, having passed the widget bundle's 36 tests and never connected the app bundle's runner. Booted first, the identical command is green in eighteen seconds. `bootstatus -b` is the half that matters: `boot` returns as soon as the request is accepted, so without it the wait is the one being avoided.

This is the same class of trap as the exit-code warning below, and the more common one: the first thing a new contributor or a coding agent does is run the documented command.

The device name is shared with CI, and was not always. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` names `iPhone 18 Pro` on an `xcode-27` runner image, the same device and the same Xcode 27.0 build (`27A266a`) a development machine has; its runtimes start at iOS 27.0, where the Pro model is `iPhone 18 Pro`. It used to name `iPhone 17 Pro`, because the `Xcode_26.6` / `macos-26` image had nothing newer and a development machine had no such device — one name would have broken whichever side lacked it. What ended that is the image, not a workaround: `xcode-27` was still marked *preview* when this moved, which is the standing cost of the match. So the commands here, in `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, both issue and PR templates, `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh`'s default and `ci.yml` now all name one device — but they name it in seven places rather than through one variable, so a future runtime bump is still a sweep. `OPENHIKES_SIMULATOR_NAME` overrides `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh`'s default, and only that script's — `Scripts/simulate-hike.sh` reads `OPENHIKES_SIMULATOR`, and defaults to `booted` rather than to a name. The two are deliberately different values rather than a drifted spelling: the UI runner resolves a device *name* to exactly one UDID through `Scripts/lib/simulator.sh` and addresses everything afterwards by that UDID, while `simulate-hike.sh` hands its `--device` straight to `simctl location`, which takes a UDID or `booted` and does not know what a device name is. So `--device <udid>` is the one spelling that means the same thing to both, and it is what a private device wants. What *is* shared, and what the parity claim is about, is the scoping.

The runner image is `xcode-27`, not `macos-26`. That is what makes the three commands above mean the same thing on a development machine and on CI: the image carries Xcode 27.0 build `27A266a` and iOS 27.0 runtimes, which is a current local install exactly. `macos-26` never offered anything past Xcode 26.6, so while `ci.yml` ran there the project was compiled by two different Swifts, and the difference was only ever visible from the red run — a nested type in an unannotated extension (see the concurrency rules below), a shadowed initializer argument in `HikeListMetricsTests`, and a `CLLocationCoordinate2D` whose members needed `import CoreLocation` that Xcode 27 supplied transitively and 26.6 did not, the last of which took down six jobs from one compile error. `xcode-27` is marked *preview* by GitHub, which warns of both instability and queueing while its capacity is balanced; that is the price of the match, and `runs-on:` plus the `env:` block at the top of `ci.yml` is the whole of the way back.

`.github/workflows/codeql.yml` is the deliberate exception and still pins `Xcode_26.6` on `macos-26`. CodeQL's Swift extractor analyses up to Swift 6.3.3 and Xcode 27 ships Swift 6.4, so that job on the new image would have no extractor rather than no findings. It moves when a bundle announces 6.4 in `swift/ql/lib/CHANGELOG.md`; the file says so at the pin.

Scope the local test command the way CI does. The `unit-tests` job passes `-only-testing:OpenHikesTests -only-testing:OpenWidgetTests`, so an unscoped `xcodebuild test -scheme OpenHikes` is not the gate CI runs — it is that gate plus the whole `OpenHikesUITests` bundle, which turns roughly twenty seconds into roughly thirteen minutes of real gestures. Run the UI automation deliberately, through `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh`, where a bare `--all` parallelises by default: about thirteen minutes of serial test execution becomes 5m49s end to end, measured on a 16-core M-series machine.

Rebase before trusting a timing. A branch cut before a fix that made a suite faster keeps paying the old cost, and a measurement taken on it describes the branch rather than the change: long after `TrailBasemapRendererTests` had its snapshot boundary injected on `main`, a stale worktree here was still spending 570 seconds in `Trail basemap rendering` and reporting it as the cost of a full test run. The same applies to a suite that got *slower*: compare against `main` at the same commit, not against a number remembered from another branch.

Unit and integration tests use Swift Testing (`@Suite`, `@Test`, `#expect`). `-only-testing:` fails **silently** in two ways, both of which report a green run having executed nothing: an identifier it cannot resolve is ignored outright — which is what a suite declared inside an `extension` looks like, so `-only-testing:OpenHikesTests/BackgroundDeliveryTests` selects nothing because that suite lives in `extension WidgetFeedSuites` — and a Swift Testing *method* needs its trailing `()`, so `…/HikeStatisticsTests/elevationGainAndLoss` runs zero tests while `…/elevationGainAndLoss()` runs it. Neither produces a warning. Any job that pins a list of `-only-testing:` entries must therefore read the result bundle and assert what actually ran rather than trust `xcodebuild`'s exit status, as the `thread-sanitizer` job does: an exact suite count, because the pinned list is fixed and a fall means an identifier stopped resolving, and a floor rather than an exact count for tests, which rise whenever anyone writes one. The `OpenHikesUITests` simulator bundle uses XCTest/XCUITest because Apple's UI automation and performance metrics are not available through Swift Testing. The main `xcodebuild test` action runs the two app-hosted bundles, `OpenHikesTests` and `OpenWidgetTests`, plus `OpenHikesUITests`; the dedicated `OpenHikesUI` scheme runs only UI automation. `OpenWidgetTests` compiles the `OpenWidget/` sources into itself, since an app extension cannot host a test bundle.

App tests use the in-memory SwiftData fixtures in `OpenHikesTests/General/TestSupport.swift`. A suite that touches the tile pipeline builds a `TileSandbox` — its own `TileCache` directories and its own `AutoSaveTileStore` — rather than `TileCache.shared`; the singletons belong to the app, and the whole bundle shares one process. Likewise `BackgroundTrailTracker`, `LocationManager` and `OfflineTileDownloader` take injectable location, defaults, clock and transport, so no test depends on wall-clock time, a real connection, or the host app's settings.

UI-test app launches pass `--ui-testing`, which selects an in-memory SwiftData store and isolated `UserDefaults`. Additional launch arguments can expand the sheet (`--ui-test-expanded-sheet`), enable real simulator Core Location (`--ui-test-enable-location`), import a bundled GPX fixture (`--ui-test-import-gpx=ThumseeLoopFast`), match against a bundled trail graph instead of Overpass (`--ui-test-trail-graph=ThumseeRidgePath`), give the tile cache its own empty storage root and no network monitor so every tile is a genuine miss (`--ui-test-offline`), seed a hike with generated photos (`--ui-test-seed-photos=<count>`), with a finished walk (`--ui-test-seed-walks=HalfLoop`, the one fixture `SeededWalkFixture` knows) or the field-metrics store with reports (`--ui-test-seed-metrics=<count>`), fail the first save of a finished recording so the retry path is reachable (`--ui-test-fail-first-save`), stand an import on the losing side of the selection race it would otherwise win (`--ui-test-lose-import-selection`), serve a fixed forecast instead of WeatherKit (`--ui-test-weather`), grant the paid-map entitlement without StoreKit (`--ui-test-entitled`), seed a fake photo library (`--ui-test-photo-library=<count>`), or answer OpenStreetMap place searches from `SeededTrailPointSource` instead of Overpass (`--ui-test-trail-points=<seeded|refused>`, three places on the `ThumseeLoopPlaces` line, or every search refused). Every one of them is `DEBUG`-only and takes effect only alongside `--ui-testing`; `AppLaunchEnvironment` is the single source of truth for all of them, and a new one belongs there and in this list beside the rest. XCUITest drives static locations through `XCUIDevice.shared.location`; longer route playback remains available through `Scripts/simulate-hike.sh`. `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` boots one UI test (`--test`), one class (`--suite … --all`) or every functional class (`--all`) against a named simulator; `--list` prints them as `Class/method`. A bare `--all` hands the fan-out to `xcodebuild`, which clones the resolved device and spreads the *classes* across the clones. That is the default rather than a flag because `--all` is the line the PR template, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, `README.md` and `AGENTS.md` all already tell a contributor to run, and an opt-in nobody types is an opt-in nobody gets. Three workers, because the floor of a parallel run is its longest class: `RecordingUITests` is 274s of a 787s serial `--all`, three already reach that floor, and a fourth only adds a device to contend with. `--serial` returns to one simulator and `--parallel N` overrides the count; the two contradict each other and passing both is an error. `--derived-data <path>` (or `OPENHIKES_DERIVED_DATA`) and `--no-device-lock` are the two a second session on the same machine needs, and the paragraph below on sharing a simulator is what they are for. Anything narrower than a bare `--all` stays serial with no comment, since a run scoped to one class or one method has nothing to spread — that is also what keeps the `accessibility-ui-tests` job on a single device, because it always passes `--suite`, and an explicit `--parallel` there is refused rather than quietly downgraded. Fixtures, launch helpers and gestures shared by the bundle live in `OpenHikesUITests/UITestSupport.swift`, and the audit types, MapKit filter and report formatting in `OpenHikesUITests/AccessibilityAuditSupport.swift` — reuse them rather than re-deriving a coordinate or a wait. The bundle is split by subject, one class per file because SwiftLint's `single_test_class` requires it: `OpenHikesUITests` (map, sheet, hike details), `OrientationUITests`, `RecordingUITests`, `TrailMakerUITests`, `WalkUITests`, `PhotoUITests`, `SettingsUITests`, `AccessibilityUITests`, and `AccessibilityLabelUITests`.

Two `xcodebuild test` runs cannot share a simulator. They install the same bundle identifier onto the same device, so the second install tears the first run's app out from under it, and the failure arrives as `Test crashed with signal kill` landing on whichever test happened to be executing — a different one each time, with no assertion and no diagnostic. Under load it also arrives as `kAXErrorServerNotFound`, `Application … is not running`, or a run that dies before any test starts. Four separate investigations this repository has run mistook that signature for a product bug, and one of them measured load average 101–180 while chasing it. If a run fails *differently* each time, or fails in an area nobody touched, suspect the device before the code: create a private device with `xcrun simctl create`, target it by UDID, and delete it afterwards — `--device` on both scripts takes a UDID as well as a name, and either way resolves to exactly one device that the destination and every `simctl` call then share. A green run on a contended simulator is no more trustworthy than a red one. The parallel `--all` is not an exception to any of this but an application of it: the fan-out belongs to `xcodebuild`, which gives each worker its own cloned device rather than letting two runs collide on one, and it clones *from* the device resolved above, so the cleared location and any `simctl privacy` grant made beforehand are inherited by every worker.

Naming that collision beats diagnosing it a fifth time, so `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` claims the device it resolved for the length of a run — a directory under `~/Library/Caches/OpenHikes/ui-test-locks` holding the run's PID — and a second run against that device is refused, naming the process that holds it, instead of being allowed to install over it. The PID is what keeps the claim recoverable: one left behind by a run that was killed is taken over rather than honoured, so a dead run cannot make a simulator permanently unusable, and `--no-device-lock` is the way past it for anyone who means it. The derived-data directory is the same problem one level down, and it is the quieter of the two: two `xcodebuild` runs against one derived-data path serialise on its build lock, and the one that waits prints nothing at all while it does — a wait here once lasted the better part of an hour and read exactly like a hang. `--derived-data <path>` gives a second session its own build, as `--device` gives it its own simulator, and `OPENHIKES_DERIVED_DATA` sets it once for a whole session the way `OPENHIKES_SIMULATOR_NAME` already does for the device. Neither has a default: every machine keeps building where it has always built until it says otherwise.

The functional UI automation does not run in CI: it drives a booted simulator through real gestures and timing-sensitive waits, which a shared runner makes slow and flaky. The accessibility classes are the exception: the `accessibility-ui-tests` job runs `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` through `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh --suite <class> --all --retry` — the `--suite` is load-bearing beyond selection, since it is what keeps a shared runner on one simulator rather than cloning three, granting location with `simctl privacy` up front so the two location-dependent tests never see a permission alert. That job ran `continue-on-error: true` from 2026-08-15 to 2026-09-06 while its flake rate was measured, and the trial is over: 192 completed runs, zero failures at the job level and at the step level both, so it now fails the workflow like every other job. The number and its one caveat — it is a *post-retry* rate, and `--retry` makes a test that passed on its second attempt indistinguishable from one that passed on its first — are recorded beside the job in `ci.yml` rather than only here. `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` names its functional classes explicitly — today `OpenHikesUITests`, `MapScreenAlertUITests`, `OrientationUITests`, `RecordingUITests`, `TrailMakerUITests`, `WalkUITests`, `PhotoUITests`, `SettingsUITests`, `CommunityUITests`, `CommunityCuratedUITests`, `CommunityPhotoUITests`, `CommunityReviewUITests`, `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests`, which is every `XCTestCase` in the bundle — for the same reason, so a new class has to be added to that list to be reachable through the script, and its `measurement_tests` list keeps `testLaunchPerformance` out of `--all` while still allowing `--test testLaunchPerformance`. A new UI test class added to that bundle inherits none of this and must be placed on the correct side of it.

`testLaunchPerformance` is the one measurement left in the bundle, and it is kept out of `--all` by `run-ui-tests.sh`'s `measurement_tests` list because a number taken on a contended machine describes the machine. Two things it learned the hard way: `stopMeasuring()` truncates `XCTApplicationLaunchMetric`'s signpost interval, which makes `harvestData` raise rather than report, so let the measure block end on its own; and absolute memory readings taken under XCUITest are automation overhead rather than the app's footprint — the same build launched by `simctl` sits substantially lower.

A UI test that spoofs a route has to respect `RecordingFixPolicy`: a static simulated location is delivered once, so a fix rejected for implied speed or displacement has to be set again, and the test waits on the `recording-point-count` element rather than on a fixed sleep. Accessibility identifiers belong on the leaf views automation taps — SwiftUI pushes a container's identifier down onto every descendant, which would leave a whole screen answering to one name.

A suite that genuinely cannot run without an environment capability (today: the App Group container) stays conditionally enabled, but must report the skip through `SuitePrecondition`; strict mode turns a missing precondition into a failure — `xcodebuild test … "SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS=\$(inherited) REQUIRE_ALL_SUITES"` from a command line, or `OPENHIKES_REQUIRE_ALL_SUITES=1` in the scheme's test action from Xcode (a simulator-hosted test bundle inherits nothing from the invoking shell, which is why there are two).

Seven jobs can fail the workflow — `Lint and shared package`, `App and widget tests`, `iOS Debug build`, `iOS Release build`, `Unsigned iOS archive`, `Thread sanitizer` and `Accessibility UI tests` — and all of them hang off a `changes` job that decides whether a pull request touched anything but `**/*.md`, `LICENSE` and `docs/`. A documentation-only pull request skips them and merges. Failing the workflow is not yet the same as blocking a merge, and this file used to claim otherwise: `main`'s branch protection lists no `required_status_checks` at all, so a red run is an annotation nobody is required to read — #182 and #185 both merged with `Thread sanitizer` red. Naming the seven there is a repository-settings change rather than a workflow one, and until it is made, "gates a merge" anywhere in this file means "reports red". The filtering is deliberately a job-level `if:` rather than a `paths-ignore:` on the trigger: a required check belonging to a workflow that never ran stays at "Expected" forever and blocks the merge outright, while a skipped *job* reports success. The list is an allow-list, so an unrecognised path counts as code and one code file among any number of prose ones runs everything; adding a new non-compiling path there is a deliberate act, not a tidy-up. A push to `main` and a manual dispatch always build everything.

Lint with `Scripts/lint.sh` (`--fix` applies what SwiftLint can correct). It runs strict SwiftLint at the version pinned in `.swiftlint-version`, and the CI `quality` job invokes that same script, so local and CI results cannot drift. It exits 0 clean, **2** for violations found and **1** for "could not run" — the third case exists because a `.swiftlint.yml` that fails to parse is only a *warning* to SwiftLint, which then lints on against the default configuration and can report a clean run having read no config at all.

The Xcode build also lints, through SwiftLintPlugins' `SwiftLintBuildToolPlugin` attached to `OpenHikes`, `OpenWidgetExtension`, `OpenHikesTests` and `OpenWidgetTests`. It runs `swiftlint lint --quiet --force-exclude` — no `--strict`, and at the version the package resolves to rather than the one in `.swiftlint-version` — so every *warning*-severity violation is invisible to it, and `Scripts/lint.sh` is what a change has to pass. An *error*-severity violation is the opposite: the plugin is a **prebuild** command, SwiftLint exits 2, and the target fails before a single file is compiled, which takes `build-for-testing` down for all four targets at once. So the error-severity rules are not advisory, they are a build gate, and these are the thresholds a large file or a branchy function actually trips: `file_length` 900, `cyclomatic_complexity` 18, `type_body_length` 450, `function_body_length` 90, `closure_body_length` 80, `line_length` 160, `identifier_name` 2–70 characters, `function_parameter_count` 9, `large_tuple` 4, and — inherited from SwiftLint's defaults rather than named in `.swiftlint.yml` — `enum_case_associated_values_count` 6. Nine more are error on a *single* occurrence: `attribute_name_spacing`, `duplicate_conditions`, `duplicate_enum_cases`, `dynamic_inline`, `force_cast`, `force_try`, `invisible_character`, `shorthand_operator` and `unhandled_throwing_task`. None of this is visible in `.swiftlint.yml`, which contains no literal `severity: error` line.

What keeps a scratch copy of the tree out of the lint is `included:`, not `excluded:` — SwiftLint's directory walk does **not** skip dot-directories, so a git worktree or a plain copy at the repository root is lintable material. `included:` stops applying the moment an explicit path is passed on the command line, which is exactly how the plugin invokes it, so `excluded:` carries `"**/.*"` as the durable guard rather than the name of whichever scratch directory exists today. `Scripts/install-git-hooks.sh` installs an opt-in pre-push hook. There is no formatting command.

Three optional tools are used if installed and skipped if not; the README lists the `brew install` line. `xcbeautify` formats `xcodebuild` output, and `Scripts/lib/xcodebuild-output.sh` is the one place that decides how — both UI scripts source it, and it falls back to their previous `grep` filter on a machine without it. Its constraint is load-bearing and is why those scripts still keep a raw log: xcbeautify prints nothing at all for output it cannot parse, which covers `measured [...]` lines, indented `PERF-` markers, ThreadSanitizer race reports, and any test failure with no recognised diagnostic — a crash or a hang produces no formatted line, not even `** TEST FAILED **`. It understands Swift Testing, so a failing `@Test` keeps its issue text and `file:line`. That raw log has a second reader: `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` names each pass's failed tests out of it, and the ones that only passed on a retry, on a green run as well as a red one. A formatted stream is a tick per test and a single mark for a failure, so a hundred green lines can carry one red one nobody sees, and a parallel run interleaves three clones through it. Both of xcodebuild's spellings are read, because they are disjoint rather than similar: a serial run prints `Test Case '-[OpenHikesUITests.RecordingUITests testSomething]' passed` and a parallel one `Test case 'RecordingUITests.testSomething()' passed on 'Clone 1 of …'`, sharing neither case, brackets nor bundle prefix — measured at six of the first and none of the second in one serial run, fifteen of the second and none of the first in a parallel one. The fallback filter in `xcodebuild-output.sh` carries only the capitalised form, so a parallel run without xcbeautify shows no test lines at all and this summary is the whole of what it reports. CI pipes every `xcodebuild` and `swift test` call through it under `--renderer github-actions` except the TSan job, whose raw report is the product; each of those `run:` blocks needs `set -o pipefail`, because Actions runs `bash -e` without it and would otherwise report the formatter's exit status rather than xcodebuild's. `Scripts/periphery.sh` runs `periphery scan` against `.periphery.yml` at the version pinned in `.periphery-version` and reports unreferenced declarations; it is not in CI because it rebuilds the project with indexing enabled, and its report is candidates to read rather than a verdict — `--exclude-tests` finds the declarations only tests use, at the cost of listing every deliberate test seam alongside them. That pin is checked as an error rather than the warning `Scripts/lint.sh` settles for, because Periphery 2.x reads none of this configuration and says so about only part of it: `--targets` was still required for an `.xcodeproj`, `retain_equatable_properties` and `retain_hashable_properties` did not exist before 3.8.0 and are reported as `invalid key`, and — because every target in `OpenHikes.xcodeproj` is an Xcode synchronized folder group rather than a list of file references — a 2.x scan with `--targets` supplied by hand indexes no Swift file at all and prints "No unused code detected" having read none of the code. The script fails a run whose output carries any of those, for the same reason `Scripts/lint.sh` fails a lint that fell back to SwiftLint's defaults. `xcode-build-server config -project OpenHikes.xcodeproj -scheme OpenHikes` regenerates `buildServer.json`, which is what lets `sourcekit-lsp` resolve symbols in the app target rather than only in the shared package; it holds absolute paths, so it is gitignored and is regenerated after adding or renaming a target.

That plugin only runs once its package fingerprint is trusted, and the trust lives per user in `~/Library/org.swift.swiftpm/security/plugins.json`, outside the repository — so a fresh CI machine fails with `Plugin "SwiftLintBuildToolPlugin" ... must be enabled before it can be used`. The checked-in `AllowedPackagePlugins.json` covers opening the project locally; CI does not read it. Every `xcodebuild` call in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` therefore passes `-skipPackagePluginValidation`, and a new one must too. Xcode Cloud composes its own `xcodebuild` invocation and cannot take that flag, so `ci_scripts/ci_post_clone.sh` — which Xcode Cloud runs by name after cloning — sets `IDESkipPackagePluginFingerprintValidatation` (Apple's typo, not ours) and `IDESkipMacroFingerprintValidation` instead. Adding a package that ships a build tool plugin or a macro needs no further change; removing the SwiftLint plugin would make all of it dead weight.

`AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` are the VoiceOver suites. The first sweeps `performAccessibilityAudit` per screen and the second asserts the labels, values and traits the app promises, because the audit cannot know that a provider row is the selected one or that the elevation graph should speak the point under the tracker. It runs with `.contrast`, `.textClipped` and `.dynamicType` subtracted — each exclusion is argued next to it, and `.dynamicType` in particular reports SwiftUI nodes it cannot introspect, including a navigation bar's own "Done" button. Issues whose detail names an `MK`-prefixed class are MapKit's and are filtered rather than fixed. Widening either exclusion needs the same argument; an audit that starts failing on a view the app does draw is a real regression.

A test that provokes a `nonisolated` delegate callback must wait through `settleDelegateHop(until:)` in `OpenHikesTests/General/SettleSupport.swift`, naming the effect it expects, rather than spinning a fixed number of `Task.yield()`s. A yield count buys an amount of progress that depends on machine load — which is how `Map coordinator` and `Location publishing` went red on CI while passing locally. Both unit bundles are `parallelizable: false` in `OpenHikes.xctestplan`, which is what makes those deadlines mean anything: the bundle is main-actor isolated project-wide, so Swift Testing's in-process parallelism could never run two tests at once, only interleave a thousand of them at their suspension points against one executor. Run 33049137656 is what that cost — seven recording tests starved together, and a five-second budget took seventeen seconds of wall time to notice it had expired. Serializing is the fix; a bigger budget is not. The condition-less overload is best-effort only, and a bare settle is almost always dead code now: because the delegate bodies deliver through `onMainActor`, a stub's `deliver(...)` runs the callback synchronously before it returns, so an assertion reading a synchronous effect (`stats`, `phase`, `trace`, a stub counter) needs no settle at all. Keep a *conditioned* settle wherever the effect is genuinely deferred — a journal flush, live matching, a shared widget snapshot, trail-graph prefetch state, the review preview, or `locationManagerDidChangeAuthorization`, which still hops explicitly because it awaits. The same rule bans a fixed `Task.sleep` as a barrier: wait on the positive effect that must follow, then assert the thing you are denying never happened.

**Tag the commit every archived build was cut from.** Nothing else in this repository can answer "which revision is build 25?" after the fact, and it cannot be reconstructed later: `SECURITY.md` states that only current `main` is supported, so there are no release branches and never will be, which makes a tag the only possible record rather than one of several. The bump commit looks like the answer and is not — `chore: bump build to 25` is followed by further commits on `main`, so whatever is submitted as build 25 is *some* commit at or after the bump, and only the person who pressed Archive knows which.

```sh
# At the commit that was actually archived, not necessarily the bump.
git tag -a v1.0-25 -m "TestFlight build 25"
git push origin v1.0-25
```

`v<MARKETING_VERSION>-<CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION>`, annotated, and a GitHub Release for the build that goes to the App Store. This is why it matters rather than why it is tidy: `General/Diagnostics/FieldMetrics/` is deliberately not `#if DEBUG`, because MetricKit only delivers against Release builds in the field, and the digest carries `appVersion` off the payload. A crash or hang report arrives naming a version, and without a tag the repository has nothing that turns that into a revision — which is the whole point of collecting them.

**Check the bundled keys before pressing Archive.** `Scripts/check-release-secrets.sh` reads `OpenHikes/Secrets.plist` and fails on an absent file, an absent key, an empty value, or a `YOUR_`-prefixed one left over from `Secrets.example.plist` — which is the likelier mistake than a missing file, and the silent one, since `Secrets.values` drops all four cases alike and returns `[:]`. The plist is gitignored, is the only place the Stadia and Thunderforest keys live, and exists on exactly one laptop; `xcodebuild archive` reports ARCHIVE SUCCEEDED with or without it, so nothing else in this repository notices. An archive cut without it ships an app whose two paid map styles cannot draw a tile — the headline features of the subscription being sold.

CI cannot hold this line and must not be made to. The `archive` job builds without keys deliberately, and its *Verify what the archive does and does not carry* step asserts everything it can; a missing `Secrets.plist` is the one thing it cannot, because in that job it is correct. A Run Script build phase conditioned on `$(CONFIGURATION)` == Release was the loudest option and loses on the `builds` job, which does a Release *simulator* build on every pull request. So this is a step a person runs, which is why it is here beside the tag rather than in `ci.yml`. The gate itself is covered by `Scripts/run-script-tests.sh` — the *Release secrets gate* block, which runs it for real against plists it writes: a file that resolves, an absent file, an absent key, an emptied one, the checked-in template unfilled, every unusable key reported at once, and a plist that is not a dictionary.

The *purchase* half of that failure is fixed in the app rather than by this check: `AboutSection` carries an **OpenHikes Pro** row that reads no entitlement, product or key, so the paywall — and with it Restore Purchases — is reachable in a build where every paid provider row is disabled. Before that row existed, `MapPaywallView` had exactly one entry point in the whole app and a missing key switched it off.

## Architecture

- Following Apple's Food Truck and Backyard Birds samples, `OpenHikes/` is organized by product domain rather than generic `Managers`, `Models`, and `Views` layers. `App/` is the composition root; `Hikes/`, `Recording/`, `Map/`, `Tiles/`, `Photos/`, `Weather/`, `Purchases/`, `Sync/`, `Settings/`, `Health/`, `Reminders/`, `LiveActivity/`, `Intents/`, `Watch/` and `General/` own their related models, services, and views. `Community/` is the seventeenth and has a bullet of its own below, because what makes it different is not where it sits. A domain folder nests once it is too large to scan, and it nests by **job**, never into `Models/`, `Views/` or `Services/` — `Hikes/` carries `Library/`, `Detail/`, `GPX/`, `Maker/`, `Places/`, `Walks/` and `Trail/`, `Map/` and `Tiles/` carry their own, and what stays at a folder's root is what all of its subfolders use. `Hikes/` keeps `Hike` itself, `RouteProfile`, `HikeTitle` and the schema there for exactly that reason.
- `OpenHikesApp` creates one `OpenHikesModel` and injects it through the SwiftUI environment. That model owns the single `ModelContainer` plus long-lived location, weather, background tracking, auto-save, cloud sync, and recording dependencies; `OpenHikesView` owns transient selection, map presentation, and navigation state. `Hike` is the persisted source of truth, while `RouteProfile` is the precomputed distance/elevation index used by both chart scrubbing and GPS route matching. Stopping a recording that the matcher moved or found ambiguous ends in `.reviewing` rather than in the store: `RouteReviewSection.sections(in:)` groups the per-fix legs into reviewable sections, `RecordingRouteReview` holds the per-section `TrailRouteChoice`, and only `saveReviewedRecording()` writes the `Hike`.
- The map is an imperative MapKit subsystem behind `MapView`. `MapView.Coordinator` observes stable controller objects and updates `MKMapView` directly. Tile drawing flows through `CachingTileOverlayRenderer` and `TileOverlay` into `TileCache`; passive durable saves go through `AutoSaveTileStore`, while policy-permitted bulk downloads go through `OfflineTileDownloader`.
- `Community/` is the one part of the app that writes to a database other people read, and is deliberately separate from `Sync/`. `Sync/` reports on SwiftData's mirroring of the hiker's own hikes into their **private** CloudKit database; `Community/` is hand-written `CKRecord` work against the **public** database of the same container, with its own transport protocol, its own record types, and no contact with the `ModelContainer` at all. It is nested by job rather than by layer, like every folder that has outgrown one level: `Transport/` is the wire — the protocol, the CloudKit, merged and seeded conformances, the schema and the three payloads; `Curated/` is the OpenStreetMap source that fills the same list without going through any of it; `Browse/` finds published hikes and draws them on the map; `Listing/` is the one a hiker opened; `Publishing/` sends a hike or a photograph out and takes it back; `Review/` is the moderator's half, plus reports and blocks. What stayed at the folder's root is what all six use. `CommunityPublisher` uploads a hike, `CommunityBrowser` holds what the searched area found, `CommunityQueryPolicy` decides whether a pan is worth *offering* to re-ask about, `CommunitySearchArea` is the circle one answer covers, `CommunityAreaName` says what to call it, `MapCommunityAnnotations` draws the results on the map that asked and `MapCommunitySearchControl` is the *Search this area* button, `MapCommunityRoutes` draws where each of those results actually *goes* — `CommunityRouteOutline` is the kilobyte-sized copy of a route that makes that affordable to fetch and `CommunityRouteHitTest` is what turns a tap on one of those lines into a hike, since MapKit hit-tests annotations and never overlays, `CommunityPageBudget` decides how many pages one request may spend once blocked rows are taken out of it, `CommunityImport` turns a published hike into an ordinary `Hike`, `CommunityReport` composes the message a hiker reports one with — which reaches the reviewer by mail rather than through the transport, for the reason given below — `CommunityBlockList` holds the authors this device has hidden, which is the browse lists' filter and needs no account, no network and no record type of its own, `CuratedTrailSource` is the OpenStreetMap half of the list and `CuratedTrailStore` is what it keeps on disk between launches, with `CommunityNearbyAnswer` carrying the scope a nearby question asks with and the `CuratedTrailOutage` a refused half reports back, and the review path is `CommunityReviewQueue` (what is waiting), `CommunityPendingSubmission` (one queue entry, carrying the fields publishing will write) and `CommunityReviewView` (where one is decided) — with the transport's reviewer half in `CloudKitCommunityTransport+Reviewing.swift`, split from its sibling for length alone. See *The community feature* below for the two record types and why there are two.
- **A trail can be drawn, and a drawn trail is an ordinary `Hike`.** `Hikes/Maker/` is the third way one is made, beside a recording and a GPX import, and it deliberately adds no fourth kind of thing: `TrailDraftSave` writes the same row an import writes, so the map, the library, the widget, GPX export, *Follow This Trail* and community publishing all reach it with nothing added to them. The consequence is stated rather than discovered — a drawn trail is an imported one plus one column, and its `date` is the day it was made. **That column is what lets it be edited**: `Hike.drawnRouteData` holds the stops, travel mode and switch it was drawn from as one JSON `DrawnRoute` (synced, because a route should be editable on the hiker's other device; `nil` on every recording and import, since re-routing a walked line would replace it with a guess). *Edit Route* on its screen (`HikeRouteEditButton` → `TrailDraftController.edit(_:)`) rebuilds the drawing from it, asking first before it replaces a different half-drawn trail; `editingHikeID` travels with the draft through `TrailDraftRecord`, so a half-finished edit resumes as one; and Save goes through `TrailDraftSave.update` into the **same** row with no name prompt — walks kept as history (the owner's decision), breakdowns emptied to be asked again, places the line no longer passes dropped with their photographs returned to the gallery (unless the maker's places switch is off; see below), the library's cached climb forgotten, and whatever the hike's places gained, lost or were renamed to while the edit stood open kept rather than overwritten by the drawing's copy (`TrailDraftSave.places(of:drawn:atOpen:)`, told apart by the ids the edit opened with). An emptied drawing is no longer an edit. A published trail may be edited; since a submission is write-once and *Share Again* is gone, `DrawnRoute.editedUnderSubmissionID` makes the share menu say the shared copy shows the old route and lead with *Ask for Removal* — a fresh share is a new submission, and the note goes by itself. The draft itself lives outside that: `TrailDraft` is the stable `@Observable` the map observes and every high-frequency write lands on, and `TrailDraftRecord` keeps it across launches in the **unmirrored** store beside `HikeLocalState`, because a half-drawn line is one device's unfinished work and mirroring it would resolve two phones drawing at once last-writer-wins. That choice is also what makes it free: no `CD_` record type, no Console index and no entry in `MirroredCloudKitSchema`. The map's pill sits in the slot `MapPhotoControlsView` occupies and is offered on the *inverse* of the `hasPushedScreen` signal the camera pill takes, so the two can never both draw without either of them knowing the other exists — see `TrailDraftController`. The record button is the lower of that pill's two, not a control in the sheet: it is the one a thumb reaches first, and the map is visible at the compact detent where the sheet draws no list. It cannot reach the sheet's navigation stack, so `RecordingEntry` starts the recorder and asks for the screen through `HikeOpenRequests`, the way a widget tap does, rather than adding a second way in. Each stretch between two points is a `TrailLeg` with a shape and a state of its own, and `OverpassTrailLegRouter` resolves it over the same `OverpassTrailGraphProvider` and `TrailMatcherGraphIndex` a recording matches against — so a drawn leg reads the z12 tiles a recording downloaded and the other way round. Legs are asked about one at a time rather than concurrently, because nineteen simultaneous requests from one phone is the shape that earns the `429` this app has already met in the field — one `AsyncStream` of leg ends read by one task in `TrailDraftController`, finished and cancelled as a unit, so a late answer is dropped by the reader's cancellation check rather than by a generation counter; a refused leg stays drawn as a straight line wearing `CuratedTrailOutage`'s own sentence and is re-asked only by *Try Again*, never by the next tap. Nothing on that path may block drawing, and Save does not wait for it. **A trail also carries the places along it, and the map can say what they are.** `Hikes/Places/` owns both halves: `TrailPlace` is the value and `TrailPoint` the mirrored row, and a drawing's places come from OpenStreetMap through the *Search this area* pill the maker borrows from the *Community* tab — the maker has no marking by hand (a hiker marks a place of their own while recording; see the saved-hike bullet below). `TrailPointQuery` is what that asks and, mostly, what it does not: `tourism=information` is 579 of the 1,206 elements every candidate tag returns over one Berchtesgaden box and 6% of them carry a name, so excluding it and `amenity=toilets` is 57% of the bytes, and areas are asked for only where a place is normally a building (`nwr` everywhere adds 749 elements of which 695 are car parks drawn as polygons). The ceiling is 10 km of radius because its box is the one those figures were measured over. **Unnamed is the normal case** — 89% of peaks carry a name against 19% of viewpoints and 5% of drinking water — so a row and a pin are built from the symbol and how far along the line the thing sits, which is also why `MKLocalSearch` cannot do this job. Answers are ranked against the *line* rather than the screen and go straight onto the trail as its places — anything within 25 m of a place already there left out — and **a save keeps only the ones the line passes**: `TrailPlaceOrder.touched(_:along:)` drops anything further than `TrailPlaceAnchor.touchedOffRouteMeters` (50 m) from the route being saved, from the hike and never from the draft, so the summit across the valley that a search found is gone from the finished trail and still there if the save is refused. The ranking runs **off the main actor**: it is places × route points, over a hundred thousand distances for forty places on a snapped route, redone after every edit and every leg that lands, so `TrailDraft` yields each request into a `bufferingNewest(1)` stream that one task reads through the `@concurrent` `TrailPlaceOrder.rows(_:along:)`, and an answer about a line that has changed since is dropped by revision. Each place carries the OSM element and the tags worth reading (`TrailPlace.osm`, `TrailPlaceFact`), which the place sheet shows and a saved hike's `TrailPoint` keeps (`osmElementType`, `osmElementID`, `osmFacts`). There is no provisional tier: the place sheet's *Remove* is how a hiker says no. **Which kinds it asks for are the hiker's**: `TrailPlaceFilter` is one switch per symbol a search can find (`TrailPointQuery.searchableSymbols`), drawn under *Follow Paths* by `TrailPlaceFilterSection`, app-wide and stored as the ones switched *off* so a symbol added later arrives on. A kind switched off is left out of the request, filtered out of any answer or stored fall-back — including one already in flight — and removed from the drawing at once by `TrailDraftController.setShowsPlaces(_:of:)`; switching it back on restores nothing, and the next search does. The switch beside the section's heading is a different kind of *off*: `TrailPlaceFilter.placesShown` hides the drawing's places rather than removing them — the pins go, the pill is withdrawn and a save attaches none of them, while the draft keeps them so *on* brings every one back — and an *Edit Route* saved with it off leaves the hike's places exactly as they were, since dropping the ones the new line misses would delete what the hiker could not see (`TrailDraftSave`'s `keepingPlaces`). The two pills are the one exclusion in this feature that does **not** fall out of an existing definition: a tab selection survives a push, so `withdrawAreaSearchForDrawing(_:)` is a rule, and the maker's is the one that stays.
- **The maker's travel mode belongs to its draft.** The icon-only segmented selector offers Hiking (the default), Walking, Cycling and Driving. Hiking uses the cached Overpass graph; the other three use `DirectionsTrailLegRouter` and `MKDirections`, with one router/cache per mode and ordered endpoints. `TrailDraftRecord.travelMode` is device-local. Mode changes preserve stops and places, clear the draft's geometry memo, and cancel the routing worker, which is also what rejects a late answer from a cancelled provider. One worker serializes requests across edits. Follow Paths remains independent and turns every mode into freehand drawing when off. Apple Maps refusals name Apple Maps and wait for Try Again; an endpoint connector longer than the hiking router's own snap radius (100 m) makes the leg visibly degraded rather than calling unchecked access a routed path — at ten metres, the first figure, nearly every leg from a stop off the road network wore the warning. A MapKit error whose underlying cause is a lost connection is *offline* and retryable, even when MapKit calls it *no route*, so a leg drawn in a dead zone is not cached as unroutable. Hosted and UI tests inject no-route directions answers at composition, never Apple's live service. The mode bar is the system's segmented `Picker`, so its segments are reached in UI tests by label through `segmentedControls["trail-draft-mode"]`, not by per-segment identifiers. **A leg can come back with alternatives, and the route has one time.** `TrailLegRoute` and `TrailLeg` carry the other ways between the same two stops (`TrailLegPath`), drawn as paler lines under the route, and a tap on one or on its bubble draws that way instead, remembered by `TrailLegMemo` like any settled shape. As in Apple Maps there is one time bubble for the whole route, halfway along its longest leg — the route's own middle is so often a stop, whose pin wins the collision and has MapKit hide the bubble — and only once no leg is still routing, and one per alternative saying what the whole trip would take that way (the trip's time less that leg's, plus the alternative's). Apple Maps' own alternatives and `expectedTravelTime` are used as given; the trail graph's are found by banning the middle half of every path already offered and asking again (Yen's k-shortest paths answers with the same path and one corner cut differently), and are offered only within 1.5× the best and sharing at most 70% of one already offered. A leg with no router estimate is timed at the mode's pace (`TrailTravelMode.paceMetersPerSecond`), which counts no climb.
- **The maker's map is diffed, not rebuilt.** A commit keeps every leg's `MKPolyline` whose leg is unchanged (matched by the id of the waypoint it arrives at) and every pin whose waypoint still exists, writing role, name and distance onto it in place — `title` and `subtitle` are stored `@objc dynamic` keys, so what MapKit and VoiceOver read follows. Rebuilding everything once per landed leg flickered every pin nineteen times for a twenty-stop route. The route choices — the grey alternatives and the time bubbles — are the one layer still redrawn whole, and only when a leg or the travel mode changes; they are inserted *below* the lowest drawn leg, because the drawn line now stays on the map across a commit and anything added afterwards would land on top of it. **While drawing on Apple's own base map, the map's labels are selectable** (`selectableMapFeatures`, points of interest and physical features): a tap on "Watzmann" drops the maker's pin headed *Watzmann* and opens the place sheet on it, and the stop it becomes arrives named, so `TrailStopNamer` never asks. The same touch also reaches the maker's own tap recognizer, in either order against MapKit's selection, so that tap does not close the card the label has just opened (`isNamedTrailDraftPin(near:in:)`). Never over OpenStreetMap tiles, which replace the map's content and would leave the labels tappable while invisible. Place search asks for `.physicalFeature` beside addresses and points of interest, so summits, passes and lakes come up by name. The search sheet's *My Location* row is always its first — disabled, and saying why, until `LocationManager.hasFix` (which changes once) or while access is refused — and reads the coordinate only when tapped.
- **A press on the canvas asks before it draws, and a place is not a waypoint.** As in Apple Maps, a press and hold on open map or on a line (`TrailDraftPinDropRecognizer`, half a second) drops a `TrailDraftDroppedPin` and opens `TrailPlaceSheet` — Apple Maps' place card, presented from inside the maker's screen with the map left live behind its smaller detents — through `TrailDraftController.selection`. A tap opens the card of whatever it lands on — a stop's pin, a place's pin, the dropped pin, a map label — chooses a grey route, and on open ground closes the card. **The pin outlives its card**: `TrailDraftController.droppedPin` is separate from `selection`, so closing the card leaves the pin standing, and it goes with *Remove Pin*, *Add Stop* or the next press. The card says where the spot is (MapKit's address, the coordinates), what OpenStreetMap says about a place, and has one verb that draws: **Add Stop**, which fills an open start or destination field and otherwise goes into the leg the pin was dropped on or the nearest one — never onto the end, so a press that meant "on the way" cannot become a new destination. The leg is remembered by its two ends (`TrailDraftDroppedPinSpot.leg`), so an edit made while the card is closed cannot move the stop into a different leg. *Share* and *Remove Pin* sit beside it — *Remove* on a place's card; a stop's card offers *Remove Stop* instead, drawn destructive. The card carries `presentationCompactAdaptation(.none)`, because a vertically compact phone otherwise presents a sheet as a full-screen cover — the rule *The primary surface has two shapes* states for the sheet itself — and a card over the whole map is a card about a spot nobody can see. **The callouts are gone and so is their race**: MapKit closes a callout it did not open itself 150–500 ms after this app's tap, which a budgeted reopen used to paper over, and a sheet is not MapKit's to close. The maker's annotations show no callout and are deselected the moment `didSelect` reaches them, because an annotation left selected swallows the next tap on it. The route tap still requires MapKit's own **double** tap to fail through `gestureRecognizer(_:shouldRequireFailureOf:)` — `mapView.gestureRecognizers` holds only this app's own recognizers, but the delegate method sees MapKit's (`MKVariableDelayTapRecognizer`) — so a double tap to zoom is not also a closed card or an opened hike. **It requires the pin-drop press to fail too**: every recognizer here recognizes alongside the others, so without it the finger that dropped a pin was also a tap as it lifted and closed the card the press had opened — seen in a UI test's screen recording. A press fails the moment a finger lifts before it began, so no tap waits for it. **The maker's own list is Apple Maps' directions list**, which is a later decision than Phase 6 and overrides two of its shapes. It opens with two empty fields, *start* and *destination*, neither filled in for the hiker — `TrailDraft.slots`, where the one fact a lone point needs beyond its place in the list is `startIsOpen` (a destination filled first stays a destination, and deleting the start of a two-point route opens the start field again), which the stored draft keeps. `slots` is **stored**, and published only when a row comes or goes: the maker's screen builds its list from it and nothing else, so a stop's name landing, a drag and a searched place filling an existing row re-run the rows that read them and not the whole screen, and `canBeSaved` is read off it for the same reason — `TrailStopSlotTests.onlyARowComingOrGoingWakesTheList` goes red with it computed. Filled rows are a start, numbered stops and a destination — `TrailStopRole`, derived from a point's place in the list and stored nowhere, so a reorder renames three rows and writes nothing — joined by a dotted stem each row draws its own half of, with *Add Stop* under them once both ends are filled; it appends, as Apple Maps' does, for the stop to be dragged into place. Every row of the route list is dragged by a press and hold, and a stop deleted with a trailing swipe, as in Apple Maps, with no Edit/Done mode, toolbar button or leading minus: iOS 27's `reorderable()` on one `ForEach` over every row, `reorderContainer(for:)` on the list, and `TrailDraft.arrangeRows(_:)` taking the order the rows now stand in. The open start and destination fields drag too and are named by where they stand — the top row is the start, the bottom the destination — so a lone point dragged under its field becomes the destination. `TrailStopReordering.swift` records what the API needs, each measured in a prototype: a single `ForEach` with no sibling `ForEach` in the section (one beside it misplaces short drags), rows that are not conditional content (or the container is never called), `listRowInsets`/`listRowSeparator` after `reorderable()`, and a data change on every drop — `.moveDisabled` and `isEnabled:` do not stop a lift, and an ignored drop leaves the list showing the wrong order. Both modifiers sit behind `#if compiler(>=6.4)` for CodeQL's Xcode 26.6 build. Stop rows print only a title — two lines at an accessibility type size — and the leg's warning glyph, when it has one; the distance along the line and the leg's notice are the row's accessibility value. **A `Menu` inside that list does not open either** — it once broke an entry nothing on screen said was broken — so the list carries none. The rule is about menus inside the list rather than toolbar menus, though the maker's toolbar carries none. **There is no undo, no redo and no ⋯ menu**, as Apple Maps' directions have none: *Reverse*, *Close the Loop* and *Clear* went with it, a stop is taken out by swiping its row and a place by its card, and the toolbar carries Save (a checkmark) and a ✕ sharing one glass pill on the trailing edge. The system back button stays on the leading edge and keeps the draft without asking; the ✕ asks, when there is a drawing, whether to *Discard Trail* or *Keep for Later*. A row is a *field*: tapping it opens `TrailStopSearchSheet`, and the place picked there fills that row and moves the camera to it, which is why the Phase 6 *Find a Place* field is gone rather than kept beside it. A row that already holds a place opens the search with its name in the field, **selected whole**, so one keystroke replaces it and one delete clears it; until the hiker types, the list under it is the empty field's — *My Location* first, then *Recents*: the places picked in this search before (`TrailStopRecents`, newest first, one row per place, at most ten, in `UserDefaults` under `maker.recentStops` and never synced), each put down again with no search, a swipe forgetting one. A *My Location* pick names nothing and is never kept. **`SearchCompleter.clear()` empties MapKit's `queryFragment` as well as cancelling**, because MapKit answers a set fragment again whenever `region` is assigned: cancelling alone left every pan after a search asking Apple about a search that had ended, and brought its places back into this sheet the next time it opened. A stop put down from an unnamed pin is named by `TrailStopNamer` a second later — one `AsyncStream` worker like the legs', one question at a time, never asked twice, a refusal never retried — and that name is a **description rather than an edit**: `TrailDraft.describe(waypointWith:as:)` moves nothing, matches by identity because the list can have moved, and `move(waypointAt:to:)` throws the name away, because a description of where a point *was* is the one thing on that row that could be false. `MKMapItem.name` is never empty — a nulled one comes back as a localized placeholder — which is why `TrailStopName` has two functions rather than one list of fallbacks: `chosen(_:)` prefers the name a hiker picked, `here(_:)` takes the address and never falls back to a name. A **place** — `TrailPlace` as a value, `TrailPoint` as the mirrored row, and *place* rather than *point* on screen because *point* already means a waypoint in the maker — is a spot on the ground rather than a rank in the line. So nothing numbers or reorders them, where each sits along the route is derived by `TrailPlaceOrder` rather than stored, and an unstated symbol is a state rather than a missing value: an imported `<wpt>` carrying a symbol this app has no glyph for keeps its name and gets no symbol, because guessing at somebody else's table would be inventing a fact about a place. `TrailPoint` is the one thing the maker adds to the mirrored schema. A saved hike's route is editable only when it was drawn here (see the bullet above); its places are editable on any hike — see the next bullet.
- **A saved hike's places are a screen of their own, and photographs are what they take.** A row of `HikePlaceSection` and a place's pin on the map (through `TrailPlacePinController.open(_:)`; no MapKit callout) push `SheetRoute.place(Hike, UUID)` — `HikePlaceView`, built from `HikePlaceCard` and the rows `TrailPlaceCardParts` shares with the maker's sheet; a tap on another pin from there replaces the screen rather than stacking one (`MapSheet.openPlace`). **What may change is the user's rule, settled 2026-09-24**: a place from OpenStreetMap (`TrailPlace.osm != nil`) takes photographs and nothing else — its name and kind are the map's, and its card links to where they are corrected — while one the hiker made (`TrailPlace.isHikersOwn`: added while recording, or read out of a `.gpx`) can also be renamed, re-kinded and annotated (`Hike.editPlace`, which refuses the other kind). Both can be removed, which returns their photographs to the hike's gallery rather than deleting them. **A place's photographs are the hike's**, linked by `HikePhoto.placeID` — a key in the `CD_photos` blob, so no mirrored column — and filed by the one path every photograph takes: the place's screen claims the map's camera pill with its place (`PhotoCaptureController.Subject.placeID`), its *Take Photo* and *Add Photos* ask the pill's own two questions, and `HikePhotoImport.add(placeID:)` files under the place only if it still exists (and re-files a picture the hike already holds). The maker's place sheet takes no photographs. ***Add Place* from the camera pill** (`HikePlaceAdder`, pushed as `SheetRoute.newPlace(Hike, HikePlaceSpot)`) is the pill's third button, on top of a pill that is a column since it arrived, and it is offered only while a saved hike's own screen holds the pill — `PhotoCaptureController.Subject.placeAnchor` is `nil` for the recording screen, which has its own *Add Place*, and for a place's screen. The spot is the photograph's rule read at the tap (`PhotoTrailAnchor.placeCoordinate`: the live match while auto-follow has one, otherwise the scrub), except that the untouched tracker answers the trailhead rather than nothing, because a place cannot go without a pin. The sheet goes to its middle detent and the map to the spot before the form arrives, and a placeholder pin (`TrailPlacePinController`'s `placeholder`, drawn even with the place switch off) stands there in the chosen kind's glyph. The form is `HikePlaceEditor`'s three questions plus *Take Photo* and *Add Photos* — no *Show on Map*, *Share* or *Remove* — starting as a viewpoint named "Viewpoint" with no note (`HikePlaceDraft`; a name that only repeats the kind is stored blank). Its photographs are held until *Add*, which is why it presents its own camera and picker rather than asking the pill's: the pill files straight into the hike, and Cancel must leave nothing behind. ***Find Places Along Trail*** (`TrailPlaceCorridorSearch`, `HikePlaceSearchSheet`) asks a finished trail the maker's save question — what the line passes, within `touchedOffRouteMeters` — by cutting the route into stretches of at most 5 km radius (at most twelve, widening to the query's ceiling past that), asked one after another through the same source and so the same `OverpassConversation`; a refused stretch is answered from `TrailPointStore` and the refusal reported beside what was found. It asks for the kinds the maker's switches leave on, offers everything found ticked, and merges by element and by `alreadyMarkedMeters`. A saved curated trail gets no places on its own; this is how it gets them. ***Add Place* while recording** (`RecordingPlaceSheet`) marks the recorder's last accepted fix: `NearbyPlaceSuggestions` offers what OpenStreetMap has within 150 m — the device's store at once, a live answer replacing it — and *your own place* never waits on that; adding opens the place's screen, so the camera is one tap away. `OpenHikesModel.placeSource` is the maker finder's source, so all three searches share one gate. **Places are published with a hike, always, and with no CloudKit schema change**: they ride in the route's own JSON asset (`CommunityRouteDocument.places`, `CommunityPlace` — strings for every enumeration, so a newer symbol or tag costs that field on an older reader rather than the decode), and a photograph's pin names its place (`CommunityPhotoPin.placeID`) only when that place is going; a contribution to somebody else's trail never names one. `CommunityRoutePayload.places(_:)` reads a stranger's list the way an imported `<wpt>` is read — off-map dropped, capped at `GPXImport.maximumPlaces`, names and notes bounded, an unknown symbol or element type answered as none — and a malformed list costs the places, never the route. The share form's disclosure counts them, the reviewer's screen lists every name and note in full (it is free text shown to strangers), the preview draws them read-only, and `CommunityImport` copies them under fresh ids, filing the author's photographs by the mapping. GPX carries a place's element as `<link href>` to its openstreetmap.org page, so a round trip keeps it OpenStreetMap's. **`CD_TrailPoint` gained `CD_osmElementType`, `CD_osmElementID` and `CD_osmFacts` on 2026-09-24, deployed to development and not yet to production**: declared by hand with `cktool import-schema` (`STRING QUERYABLE SEARCHABLE SORTABLE`, `INT64 QUERYABLE SORTABLE` and `BYTES QUERYABLE SORTABLE`, the shapes the existing columns of those Swift types mirror to) and verified by re-export, development `md5 a5c58437975dcaf839db084d4ff026d7`. Production exported `831b5dc5c9507a73305ff398507a7e08` that day, which is development without those three lines, so it needs the Console promote. Hand-declared shapes are inferred rather than observed, so a development build that saves a place from OpenStreetMap and mirrors it without error comes before the promote. **`CD_Hike` gains `CD_drawnRouteData` with *Edit Route*** (a `Data?` column with no external storage, so `BYTES QUERYABLE SORTABLE` like the other data columns and no `_ckAsset` beside it), declared by hand in development on 2026-09-24 and not yet in production — see the end of the Community section for the numbers.
- `OpenHikesShared` is a local Swift package consumed by the app and iOS widget. Its source and tests mirror the `Recording/`, `Trails/`, `Widget/`, `LiveActivity/`, `Intents/` and `General/` domains; put cross-target payloads, projections, deep links, and shared presentation logic there rather than duplicating them in targets.
- The app precomputes a compact `SharedTrailSnapshot`, writes it atomically through `SharedStore`, and reloads widget timelines. The iOS widget reads that App Group store directly and never recomputes route matching — but it does read location, deliberately, which the next bullet describes. Both snapshots use the current wire format described in *Schema and migration policy*. Every version mismatch or decode failure is reported as a `SharedStoreDiagnostic` to the `OpenHikes`/`SharedStore` log with the offending key and coding path named; the shared package uses `os.Logger` throughout. `TrailBasemapSet` carries no version deliberately — it is regenerable derived state, so a schema change costs one render rather than a blank widget — but its decode failures are reported the same way, because an undecodable manifest re-renders forever. A partly failed render pass publishes the images that did land rather than discarding all four: the four snapshots are four separate requests, and the widget picks one image by shape and appearance, so a set holding the one it is being asked for draws a map where an all-or-nothing set draws the line glyph. That is only safe because `refreshIfNeeded`'s short-circuit asks `TrailBasemapRenderer.holdsEveryCombination(_:)` as well — its other three questions (same coverage, images on disk, intended scale) are all asked of the manifest's *own* images, so without it a manifest holding three of four would be accepted as done forever and the missing combination would fall back to the line glyph until the trail's geometry changed. **The container keeps a basemap set per trail, not one in total.** A widget pinned to a trail draws that trail whatever is selected, so its map has to outlive the selection: when there was one manifest, selecting another trail replaced it and pruned the old images, and every pinned widget drew its line on a grey fill under its own figures. Now `saveBasemapSet` writes `basemap-sets/<hike>.json`, the selection's render and `TrailBasemapRenderer.invalidate()` prune every set except the pinned trails' (asked of `WidgetCenter` through `SharedHikeCataloguePublisher.pinnedTrails()`), and the launch sweep renders any pinned trail's map that is missing, in a lane of its own that a selection change does not cancel. `SharedStore.clear()` no longer touches basemaps for the same reason. When WidgetKit cannot say what is pinned (`PinnedTrails.unknown`), the basemap prunes delete nothing, which is the opposite of what the snapshot prune does: a missing snapshot comes back on the next sweep, but a deleted map costs four network renders and a grey widget until then.
- **What the Home Screen widget draws, and where each figure comes from.** A rendered basemap fills it edge to edge; across the top sit the current temperature on the left and the trail's climb and length on the right, stacked one per line because side by side they truncated to nothing on `systemSmall`; along the bottom sits the progress bar. Nothing is drawn in the middle and there is no status line any more — the sentence it used to carry (`SharedTrailSnapshot.statusText`, still the accessibility value and still the Lock Screen's) said a percentage and a distance left, which is the same fact the bar now shows at a glance and without taking a band out of the map. `TrailWidgetLayout.metricLimit` therefore starts at **two** rather than one: the climb and the length are what the corner exists to say, and the third chip — the hiker's own height for a trail, the pace for a recording — is the one a `systemSmall` gives up. The recording state draws the same top line with its own figures and deliberately **no bar**, because it has no length to be a fraction of; every bar that could be drawn for it would be inventing a denominator. The temperature is the one figure that is not per-trail: it is whatever the app's weather badge is showing, published to `weather-reading.json` by `WeatherWidgetPublisher` and carried by the entry through the recording takeover, since it belongs to the badge rather than to the trail. It is dropped past `SharedWeatherReading.maximumAge` — three hours, far looser than the half-hour the badge *dims* at, because the badge sits beside an app that is polling and the widget is a picture redrawn every six hours — and `TrailWidgetProvider.nextReload` folds `expiresAt` into the refresh date so the entry that drops it is scheduled rather than stumbled upon. The publisher writes every reading and asks for a redraw only when the *drawn string* would change, which at whole degrees most refreshes do not; it is not gated by `requestUnlessRecording()`, because unlike a trail redraw during a recording this one is never byte-identical.
- **The widget gallery draws checked-in basemaps.** The placeholder trail does not exist, so nothing has ever rendered it into the App Group and `TrailMapView` fell all the way back to the line glyph — a hiker choosing the widget saw a squiggle where a real trail shows a map. `Scripts/placeholder-basemaps.sh` renders the same four images the app's renderer would, once, into `OpenWidget/Assets.xcassets`, and `TrailWidgetBasemapImages` is the reader that tells a data-set name from an App Group file name. The route it frames is above the Königssee, the same valley the App Store screenshots are staged in, because four rendered images of the Cupertino street grid it used to run through is a hiking widget advertising itself with a map of parked cars. Nothing rebuilds them: `placeholderBasemapsFrameTheTrail` in `OpenWidgetTests` asserts every point of the placeholder route still lands inside every image, which is what fails when the route moves and what names the script to re-run.
- The widget *does* read location, and that is a shipped feature rather than an oversight: `OpenWidget/Info.plist` declares `NSWidgetWantsLocation` and `TrailWidget.swift` owns `WidgetRecordingLocationSampler`, which drops the sparse anchors the README advertises into a live recording so the app can repair a GPS gap it slept through. It is fenced in on every side. The timeline provider asks for a fix only when the stored `SharedRecordingSnapshot` says `isCapturingFixes`, and awaits it best-effort — a timeline is owed whether or not a fix arrives, so both paths end in `Self.currentTimeline()` and the entry is re-read from the store afterwards. The sampler itself refuses unless `CLLocationManager.isAuthorizedForWidgetUpdates` holds and the status is `.authorizedAlways` or `.authorizedWhenInUse`, takes at most one fix per 15 minutes through `SharedStore.claimRecordingWidgetSample` — a lock-file claim in the App Group rather than an in-process timer, because a widget process is short-lived and there can be several — and gives up after 8 seconds. `WidgetRecordingRequest.consume()` is what makes the race between an arriving fix and that timeout resume the continuation exactly once, which is the precondition `withCheckedContinuation` needs. A fix that survives `WidgetRecordingFixPolicy` — at most 5 minutes old, horizontal accuracy between 0 and 200 m, Mercator-representable — is appended through `PendingRecordingFixStore.append(_:validatingRecordingAt:)`, which re-reads the snapshot under the same lock and drops the fix if the session changed or the recording stopped meanwhile; the queue is `pending-fixes.json`, capped at 200 entries oldest-first. Elevation rides along only when `verticalAccuracy` is within 30 m, course and speed only when non-negative.
- That hand-off is one-way, and the widget's half of it is append-only: it never reads the queue back, never matches a route and never computes a statistic, which is the boundary it really keeps. `HikeRecorder.mergePendingWidgetFixes(for:)` drains it — `AppGroupRecordingSharedStateStore.pendingFixes(for:)` filters to the live session off-main, `journalQueue.drain()` settles the journal first so the merge sees every fix already accepted, `TrackJournal.mergeWidgetFixes` deduplicates against the journal's timestamps within 5 seconds, and `removePendingFixes(ids:)` clears what merged. Failing that last clear is logged rather than fatal on purpose: the journal merge is already durable, and the next drain deduplicates the copies left behind.
- The Live Activity is split across all three targets along the same seam the widget is. `OpenHikesShared/LiveActivity/` owns `HikeActivityAttributes` — the payload — plus its content builders and `HikeActivityPresentation`, which decides every word, rounding and chip on both surfaces and is the testable half of the UI. `OpenWidget/` draws it. `OpenHikes/LiveActivity/` decides *when* one exists. The payload is a plain `Codable, Hashable, Sendable` struct and its `ActivityAttributes` conformance lives alone in `HikeActivityAttributes+ActivityKit.swift` behind `#if os(iOS)`: ActivityKit *is* importable on macOS, but `ActivityAttributes`, `Activity` and `ActivityContent` are all `@available(macOS, unavailable)`, so `canImport` is the wrong guard and the package's macOS support — which is what lets `swift test` run the shared package's test suite on a Mac in CI — would otherwise have to go. The attributes *type name* is a storage contract: ActivityKit identifies a running activity by it, so renaming the type orphans every activity already on screen.
- A Live Activity never reads the App Group store, a location or a route profile; it renders `context.state` and nothing else, exactly as the widget renders its snapshot. Both surfaces are fed from the same two funnels the widget is fed from — `HikeRecorder.publishSharedRecordingSnapshot(force:)` and `BackgroundTrailTracker.updateStoredLiveFix` — so the two can only ever disagree about a *rate*, never about a fact. The polyline is deliberately left out of the payload: attributes plus `ContentState` share a 4 KB budget, and `payloadFitsTheActivityBudget` asserts it. `ContentState` carries `elapsedSeconds` and `updatedAt` so the view can derive a `timerStart` and hand the ticking to `Text(timerInterval:)`, which the system advances without spending an ActivityKit update; `RunState` is what says whether that timer may run, because a `Text(timerInterval:)` cannot be stopped once drawn.
- **A hike's name is bounded where it is entered, not where it is spent** (`Hikes/HikeTitle.swift`). It is the only free text the app carries from a person or a file into the 4 KB payload above, and `HikeTitle.bounded(_:)` is the one place the rule lives — the rename field, the Stop alert's name field (through `HikeRecorder.normalizedCustomName`) and the GPX importer (through `HikeTitle.imported(trackName:fileURL:)`) all go through it, and a new way to name a hike has to as well. Both bounds are load-bearing: 128 characters *and* 512 UTF-8 bytes, because a grapheme cluster has no length limit, so a character count alone would let one `Character` of ten thousand combining marks through — not a thing anybody types, which is exactly why an unattended `Documents/Inbox` file is what it is for. The shared package's `HikeActivityTests` measures its worst case at 498 bytes against these numbers and cannot import the app to check them, so the two move together.
- Target folders are Xcode file-system-synchronized groups. New Swift files under `OpenHikes/`, `OpenHikesTests/`, `OpenHikesUITests/`, `OpenWidget/`, `OpenWidgetTests/`, `OpenHikesWatch/` or `OpenHikesWatchWidgets/` are discovered by their corresponding targets; place files in the target that should compile them. `OpenWidget/` is synchronized into two targets — the extension and `OpenWidgetTests` — with `OpenWidgetBundle.swift` excluded from the latter, since a test bundle must not carry a second `@main`. A folder synchronized into a target has its *resources* bundled too, and flat — which is why `OpenHikes/SimulatedLocations/` needs `EXCLUDED_SOURCE_FILE_NAMES = "*/SimulatedLocations/*"` on the app target's **Release** configuration alone. The four fixtures there are read from `Bundle.main` by `--ui-test-import-gpx=` and `--ui-test-trail-graph=`, so Debug must keep them and a shipped build must not carry test data it has no `#if DEBUG` code left to read. `OpenHikes.storekit` is the same question answered a different way: it is not in the synchronized folder at all, so it was in the app's Resources phase by hand and is now in neither — the scheme's `StoreKitConfigurationFileReference` names it by path and never wanted it copied into the product. What keeps both out is project configuration, which fails silently; CI's archive job asserts the absence, reading the fixture names off the folder so a fifth one is covered on the day it is added.

## Repository-specific conventions

- Preserve render isolation.
