High-frequency GPS, sheet, chart-scrub, route-styling, and map-command state lives in stable `@Observable` reference types such as `RouteHighlight`, `SheetMetrics`, `RouteStyle`, `MapController`, `TrackerState`, and `LocationManager`. Parent SwiftUI bodies must not read their changing properties; `MapView.Coordinator` uses `withObservationTracking` to update only MapKit. `Self._logChanges()` in the body under suspicion is what names the input that differed, when changing this flow.
- UI and SwiftData coordination are main-actor isolated. Delegate callbacks are `nonisolated` and reach that state through `onMainActor { ... }` in `General/MainActorDelivery.swift`, which runs the body synchronously via `MainActor.assumeIsolated` when the callback already arrived on the main thread and falls back to `Task { @MainActor in ... }` when it did not. Every `CLLocationManager` here is created on the main actor, so its deliveries take the synchronous path — which is what removes a heap allocation per GPS fix across three live delegates, and what restores ordering between consecutive batches, since two separate unstructured tasks on one actor have no defined order and a reordered pair is silently dropped by `RecordingFixPolicy`'s `interval > 0` guard. A callback that has to `await` (authorization changes, `withObservationTracking` re-arming) keeps the explicit `Task { @MainActor in ... }`; a `withObservationTracking` `onChange` **must** stay deferred, since it fires mid-mutation. Tile math, image encoding, disk enumeration, and other blocking pipeline work stay off the main thread; existing hot paths call `assertOffMainThread`. Keep shared off-main types `Sendable` and protect mutable singleton state with the existing lock pattern.
- Going the *other* way needs `Task.detached` or a `nonisolated` function, never a bare `Task {}`. A `Task {}` started from a method on a `@MainActor` type inherits that isolation and runs its body on the main thread, so any synchronous call inside it blocks the UI while looking exactly like offloaded work. This shipped once: `CloudSyncCoordinator` built its `CKContainer` inside such a task, and CloudKit's framework load and daemon handshake pinned the main thread for seconds on a fresh install — a grey map, no sheet, and an unresponsive app on a new user's first launch. `CloudSyncCoordinator.offMainThread(_:)` is the guarded seam and `CloudSyncCoordinatorTests` fails if either safeguard is removed. Making a property `lazy` does not help: it changes *when* the work runs, not *where*. A bare `nonisolated` *function* is only half the escape, and the other half is the one that bites: `SWIFT_APPROACHABLE_CONCURRENCY` makes a `nonisolated async` function `nonisolated(nonsending)`, so it runs on its caller's executor — a main-actor caller means a main-thread body. Say `@concurrent` on the callee, and on a protocol *requirement* when the off-main-ness is part of the contract rather than of one conformance. `PhotoLibraryWriting.save` is why that is written down: it cost a `MainThreadWatchdog` stall for PhotoKit's first-touch handshake and, worse, a crash — a `performChanges` block formed inside a main-actor body inherits main-actor isolation, PhotoKit runs it on `com.apple.PHPhotoLibrary.changes`, and the isolation check Swift emits at the top of it trapped every mirrored save. `PhotoLibraryMirrorTests.mirroringStaysOffTheMainActor` reads the executor the stub's body actually woke up on, and the stub stays free of `@concurrent` so it cannot pass by hopping under its own power. **Spell `nonisolated` on the extension, not on the type and then nowhere else.** `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor` makes an unannotated extension a main-actor context even when the type it extends is `nonisolated`, and Xcode 26.6 and 27 disagree about what that means for a *nested type* inside one: 27 reads it as nonisolated, 26.6 as main-actor, and refuses the build. `MergedCommunityTransport` shipped four red CI jobs that way while every local gate was green, back when CI ran 26.6 and nothing local could see it. CI runs the same Xcode 27 as a development machine now, so this particular trap no longer fires — the rule stands anyway, because where it *did* compile the helpers ran on the main actor, which for merge and disk work is a real defect and not a compiler opinion. Every extension of `CloudKitCommunityTransport` says `nonisolated`, and that is the pattern rather than an ornament.
- Respect tile-provider policy. `TileProvider.supportsBulkDownload` gates prefetching: OpenStreetMap is passive auto-save only. Tile identity is provider plus zoom/x/y and nothing else — display scale is deliberately absent, because no provider template substitutes one and both paths therefore fetch identical bytes; `TileCacheKey` defines the shared spelling for the renderer and downloader. When deleting durable tiles, use `TileOwnership` so tiles shared by multiple hikes are not removed.
- Present modals from inside the sheet's *contents*, not beside the presentation. `OpenHikesView` keeps `MapSheet` presented permanently in portrait and puts it back if it is ever dismissed, so a `.sheet`, `.fullScreenCover`, `.photosPicker` or `.fileImporter` attached to the same view as that sheet is never presented at all — no error, just a button that does nothing. `MapSheet`'s `.fileImporter`, and the `.photoCapturePickers`, `.weatherDetailSheet` and `.mapScreenAlerts` on `OpenHikesView.mapSheet()`, are inside for this reason. **Alerts are not an exception**, and this line said they were until a hiker found out otherwise: an alert raised while the sheet was settled opened *and took the sheet down for the rest of the launch* — `showSheet` stays `true`, so the `onChange` that re-presents it never fires — while one raised as the sheet was going up was swallowed with no trace at all, which is why the first failure went unreported. Every alert the map screen raises is in `MapScreenAlerts`, and `MapScreenAlertUITests` is what keeps it there. "Inside the contents" rather than "inside the sheet" is what keeps one answer right in both shapes below: in landscape there is no sheet to be beside.
- **The primary surface has two shapes, and landscape is not the sheet.** `.presentationDetents` are honoured only in a compact-width, *regular*-height presentation, so in compact height — iPhone landscape — the system ignores them and presents the sheet full-screen. For a sheet that is never taken down that is not a taller sheet but the whole UI, with the map behind it and nothing that brings it back; it shipped that way, and `OrientationUITests` is what stops it coming back. `MapSidePanel` is drawn beside the map instead — an ordinary overlay, not a presentation, holding the same `MapSheet` — while `SheetPresentation.layout` resolves what the two shapes disagree about, so no screen inside the sheet asks which one it is in. **`verticalSizeClass` is read in `SheetLayoutReader` and nowhere else**, and that is a render-isolation rule rather than tidiness: an `@Environment` read in `OpenHikesView`'s body re-runs it whenever SwiftUI thinks the value may have moved, which a scene transition does — measured as one extra root body pass per transition (`testBackgroundRecordingCostsNothingPerFix` fails by exactly that one), the map update that follows it, and 250-odd tile requests in an offline browse budgeted for none. The flag it publishes changes on a rotation and at no other time. For the same reason the sheet is presented from `$showSheet` rather than from a `Binding` built in the body, which is a new binding on every pass and re-runs the sheet's content with it. Two things follow. The map's own controls hang off a layout guide the panel's width is spent on (`MapView.sidePanelInset` → `Coordinator.controlsLeadingConstraint`), because `additionalSafeAreaInsets` belongs to `UIViewController` and this map is a `UIView`. The camera's route fitting spends that same occupied width on the physical leading edge, including the panel's safe-area margin. **Only the map may ignore the horizontal safe area**: the weather overlay and panel share the window's safe leading edge, while the badge ignores only the vertical safe area, so `WeatherBadge.topPadding` is measured from the map's own top edge. `OpenHikesApp`'s scene root keeps the safe area. `SheetPresentation` retains each destination's `HikeDetailInteraction` and `PhotoViewerSelection` until its route is popped, so replacing the host on rotation preserves the selected section, rename draft and current photo; these objects are read by the destination, never by the root or sheet bodies.
- Files written outside SwiftData need an owner and a sweep. Photo and tile deletion is fire-and-forget, so termination can leave files with nothing pointing at them; `TileCache.trimCache(claimedBy:)` and `HikePhotoStore.reclaimOrphans(claimedBy:)` are the backstops, both driven at launch from a *complete* claim set — a fetch that fails must sweep nothing rather than sweep with an empty set.
- **A program inside YAML is a program nothing checks.** Anything a workflow decides with more than a shell conditional goes in a file under `Scripts/`, not in a heredoc: the coverage floor and the ThreadSanitizer suite-count gate spent months as heredocs, where no parser read them, nothing linted them and no test could reach them, while one of them could fail a merge. They are `Scripts/check-coverage-floor.sh` and `Scripts/check-sanitized-selection.sh` now, and the pins they enforce stay in the workflow as environment variables, next to the comments that argue for the numbers. Shell is the only scripting language in this repository — the `quality` job parse-checks every `*.sh` under `Scripts/` and `ci_scripts/` with the interpreter its own shebang names, and `Scripts/run-script-tests.sh` runs each gate against fixtures it writes itself.
- `TileCache` intentionally has memory, ephemeral cache, and durable Application Support tiers. Do not turn a render miss into synchronous disk/network work, and do not move expensive storage measurement into a SwiftUI body.
- The paired SwiftData stores open through `ModelContainer.openHikes(...)` with the current `OpenHikesSchema`. See *Schema and migration policy* for the reset contract and CloudKit requirements.
- iCloud sync is SwiftData's own CloudKit mirroring, not a sync engine this repo owns. `Hike` lives in a store built with `cloudKitDatabase: .automatic`; everything describing files in *this* device's Application Support lives in `HikeLocalState`, a second `@Model` in a second, unmirrored `ModelConfiguration`. That split is load-bearing, not cosmetic: `TileOwnership` builds its claim set from `offlineDownloads` and `autoSavedTileKeys`, and `TileCache.trimCache(claimedBy:)` deletes whatever no hike claims, so mirroring those columns last-writer-wins would strip a second device of tiles it genuinely downloaded. `ModelConfiguration+OpenHikes.swift` is the only place `cloudKitDatabase` is named — build containers through its `ModelContainer.openHikes(...)` factories rather than with a `ModelConfiguration(` literal. Cross-store relationships are illegal, so the two rows join on `hikeID` by value and deleting a hike must call `hike.deleteLocalState()` by hand, *after* any tile-deletion plan has been built from the claim set it is about to remove. A new device-local column belongs in `HikeLocalState` with a passthrough on `Hike`; a new synced column belongs on `Hike` with an inline default. `CloudSyncCoordinator` only reports and toggles: it reads `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer.eventChangedNotification`, reduces each event to a `Sendable` `CloudSyncOutcome` on the posting thread, and surfaces `pendingRelaunch` because a `ModelConfiguration` cannot change its mind mid-launch. Letting SwiftData own sync gave four things up deliberately, and none of them is a bug to be found later: photo pixels are files rather than columns and do not travel, so a second device gets a photo's metadata and no file behind it — which the gallery, the map callout and the viewer say in as many words rather than drawing a broken picture, and which is now a decision rather than an open question (see *Settled decisions*); a rename re-uploads the whole row including routes; a recording in progress is a row like any other, so a second device can show a hike whose line is still being drawn; and there is no hook to prefer an unsent local edit over an incoming one. Sync also cannot be exercised between two simulators the way a device pair works — the Simulator receives no CloudKit push, so a second one only picks up changes when it is brought to the foreground.
- **Recording draft cleanup requires positive local ownership.** `Hike.isRecording` is mirrored, but `TrackJournal` is device-local. `HikeLocalState.ownsRecordingDraft` is set only when this device creates a journal or recovers a matching one, saved alongside the draft, and required by the automatic orphan sweep. Tiles, photos and a sidecar row do not establish ownership. An absent journal is never evidence that this device owns a draft; a matching recovered journal can establish ownership.
- Remember only the *negative* entitlement answer. `MapEntitlementStore` persists its resolved answer under `SettingsKey.lastKnownMapEntitlement` and seeds `.notEntitled` at init when that answer was negative, but leaves state `.unknown` when it was positive. The asymmetry is the point: `.unknown` is already permissive, so a subscriber's map never flickers locked on a cold launch before StoreKit answers, while a non-subscriber is never served billed tiles in that window. Seeding the positive too would make a lapsed subscription paint an unlocked map until StoreKit disagreed. The store takes injectable `defaults`; `OpenHikesModel.entitlementDefaults(_:)` hands the app-hosted test bundles a wiped suite so a stub never writes into the developer's real defaults.
- **Following a trail is a walk, and the walk outlives the screen.** `TrailWalkSession`, owned by `OpenHikesModel`, is the one place a walk starts (on the first matched fix in `HikeDetailView.updateLiveFollow`, with Follow This Trail on and never for a recording's draft), accrues (the coverage union in `TrailWalkCoverage` — intervals consecutive matches spanned, never bridged across more than 500 m, so the figure is coverage rather than position), pauses, and ends into a `HikeWalk` row. Because nothing is tapped to start one, the start is said on the map: `TrailWalkSession.startNotice` is set by an auto-start and by nothing else — not by a walk a relaunch adopts — and `WalkStartedPill` draws it under the weather badge until its *x* or the walk's end clears it, with a tap that opens the trail's Pause and End. The walk in progress is a `Codable` column on `HikeLocalState`, device-local like the tile claims and written at milestones and the 45-second publish cadence, never per fix; the finished row is mirrored and hangs off `Hike.walks` with a cascade, and `SheetRoute.walk` is popped with its hike. One walk at a time: while one is active or paused `BackgroundTrailTracker` pins `trackedHikeID` to it and defers selection changes until it ends, so the widget, the Lock Screen and background matching all belong to the walk, and a background relaunch restores it from the sidecar in the model's `init` — before any view — because a fix in a relaunched process has to find the walk it belongs to. Popping the detail, comparing another trail, starting a recording or turning Follow This Trail off changes no walk phase. The toggle controls the live chart position, map pin ownership and permission to auto-start a new walk; enabling it rearms auto-start after an End. An existing walk keeps accruing from both feeds with the toggle off, and keeps its widget and Lock Screen panel. Pause / Resume / End own the walk's manual phase changes, and Resume preserves the toggle's value. Recording is untouched by all of it: the recorder stays the single authority on its draft, the precedence rule below still has exactly three homes, and `TrailWidgetReload.requestUnlessRecording()` still gates the trail feed's redraws. The one `HikeWalk` a walk session does *not* write is the recording's own: `HikeRecorder.persist(_:prepared:customName:)` writes one row per saved recording through `HikeWalk.recorded(_:prepared:)` in `RecordedWalk.swift`, in the same commit that finalizes the draft and rolled back with it if the store refuses, so a recorded hike's History leads with the walk that made it. It carries `TrailWalkEndReason.recorded`, covers the whole route by construction, and is measured against `PreparedRecording.routeLengthMeters` — the plain sum along the saved line, which is what `RouteProfile` measures and therefore the only scale a walk's coverage may be written on; `Hike.distanceMeters` is the hiker's figure, with stationary windows retracted, and a walk written against it would read as a walk along a trail that has since changed. Its active time is `PreparedRecording.recordedSeconds` — the gaps between consecutive saved points, less the leg a pause boundary opened — and **not** wall clock minus `TrackJournalMetadata.pausedIntervals`, which is not a complete record of when a recording was not running: `finishRecovery` parks a recovered session in `.paused` / `.needsDecision` without writing a pause, and no interval exists at all for the stretch between a killed process and the relaunch that finds the journal. It is also the one walk exempt from `TrailWalkPolicy.minimumCoverageMeters`, since a recording the hiker saved is never the glance at a trailhead that rule exists to discard.
- **A reminder is one controller's decision, and its categories are a storage contract.** `MovementReminderController` is handed to the recorder and to the walk session the way `HikeLiveActivityController` is, and for the same reason: *a recording outranks a followed trail* is only expressible by something that can see both, and two controllers would be two banners about one walk. The thresholds live in `MovementReminderPolicy` and nowhere else — five hundred metres from where the pause began, or two hundred and fifty inside two minutes for the bicycle case the issue was raised about, at most three reminders per pause with a quarter of an hour and another crossing between them, and a quarter of an hour of `RecordingDistanceAccumulator.isStationary` before a *running* recording suggests pausing. Displacement from the anchor rather than an accumulated total, because a phone left on a table accumulates half a kilometre of GPS wander and displaces nothing. `MovementReminderKind`'s raw values spell both the notification and the category identifiers, and a delivered notification carries its category for as long as it sits in Notification Centre — so renaming one leaves a hiker holding a banner whose Resume button reaches a delegate that no longer recognises it. The buttons themselves go through `HikeIntentCoordinator`, so a notification action, Siri and the Control Center toggle cannot drift apart; the banner's own tap is left to the system, since routing to a screen is view state a delegate has no way to set. `makeMovementReminderController(defaults:)` returns `nil` under `isRunningTests` rather than `isHostingTests` — UI tests are excluded too, because the authorization prompt is a system alert and a run cannot tap its way past one. **A walk also says how long it has left, and whether that runs past dark.** `WalkTimeLeft` is DIN 33466 (`WalkingTimeEstimate`) over the distance the walk has not covered and what the line climbs from the hiker to the end they are heading for — a walk can run the route backwards, which the coverage says, and then the stored climbs are descents — scaled — once the walk has covered a kilometre in a quarter of an hour — by the walk's own active time over what the same rule says its covered stretches should have taken, bounded to 0.5–2×. No heights and no calibration is no figure. The session keeps the profile its walk started with (a walk adopted at launch has none until the detail's follow loop hands one in), and the figure rides on `SharedTrailSnapshot.Walk.secondsLeft` to the Lock Screen's *Time left* chip, beside the distance left on the phone's readout. `DuskWatch` posts `.afterDark` once per walk, at the moment the estimate first passes **civil dusk** — at the crossing with no slack, the owner's decision — never after dusk has passed and never with no dusk to cross; the dusk is the badge's reading when it is about the hiker or the selected trail (`WeatherBadgeState.daylightNearHiker`). A recording has no route to measure against and suppresses it, as it does every walk reminder.
- **A recording always outranks a followed trail**, and one `HikeLiveActivityController` instance is what makes that expressible — the recorder and the tracker are handed the same object. A recording is the thing that would be *lost*; a follow is a convenience the hiker can recreate by selecting the trail again. The controller also owns every rate decision: a 20-second update floor, a 10-second floor on the status flips that bypass it (pausing, losing the trail), stale dates of 10 minutes for a recording and 30 for a follow, and a 5-minute lingering final panel for a *finished* recording only. A discarded recording leaves nothing behind — `end(subject:finalState:dismissAfter:)` treats a `nil` final state as "take it off screen now", and substituting the current state there once silently defeated the discard path. A follow starts only on a *matched* fix, never on mere selection, but keeps updating on an unmatched one so "off the trail" can be said.
- There are no buttons on the Live Activity. The whole panel is a deep-link tap target reusing `TrailWidgetDeepLink`, which lands on the controls that already work; adding a `LiveActivityIntent` remains a separate interaction change rather than part of the Control Center control.
- App Intents run in the app's process but not in its view hierarchy. The system can launch this process purely to perform one, so nothing built by a `.task` or held in the environment is reachable: `OpenHikesApp.init()` registers a `HikeIntentCoordinator` with `AppDependencyManager` and every intent in `OpenHikes/Intents/` is a title, a phrase and one call into it. That coordinator is the *whole* of what an intent can do, and it owns no state — the recorder remains the single authority on whether a hike is being recorded, since the widget, the Live Activity and the recording screen all read it and a fourth answer kept beside them could only ever disagree. It also imports no AppIntents, which is what lets a suite drive start/pause/resume/stop through a real `HikeRecorder` with a stub location source and no ActivityKit, App Group or Core Location behind it. A suite reaches the intents themselves through `HikeIntentContext.$override`, a `@TaskLocal` read in preference to the `@Dependency`: asking `AppDependencyManager` for something never registered traps rather than returning nil, and a plain global would let one test's recorder answer another's intent under parallel execution. The registration is behind the `isRunningTests` guard for the reason the other startup writers are. Recording intents declare `IntentModes.background` — the hiker's hands are busy and the phone is in a pocket — and start and resume add `.foreground(.dynamic)` and *use* it: they `continueInForeground(_:)` when `HikeIntentAuthorization.needsForeground` holds, then carry on in the same `perform()`. Two of Core Location's prompts are foreground-only and the recorder walks into both — `start()` calls `requestWhenInUseAuthorization()` for `.notDetermined`, and `activateSessionIfPossible()` and `resume()` each call `requestTemporaryFullAccuracy()` and then fail with `.preciseLocationRequired` — so `.reducedAccuracy` is reported separately from `.granted` rather than folded into it. `continueInForeground` rather than `needsToContinueInForegroundError`: that error re-*runs* `perform()`, and the re-run would find the same undecided authorization, because nothing between the two runs asked Core Location. The recorder reports refusals by moving to `.failed` rather than by throwing, so an intent that merely awaited `start()` would confirm a hike that never began; `HikeIntentCoordinator` reads the phase back and is where that stays fixed. Every phase-reading entry point awaits `HikeRecorder.settleAutomaticRecovery()` first: a launch that recovers automatically enters `.recovering` *synchronously* in `init`, whether or not there is anything to recover, and the launch these intents exist for is the one the system makes in order to perform one — so an unguarded read answers about the launch ("still finishing your last recording") rather than about the hiker's hike. Everything the coordinator speaks is spoken: `HikeIntentFailure` carries no SwiftData or store diagnostics, which are logged to `OpenHikes`/`Intents` instead, durations go through `HikeFormat.spokenDuration(_:)` rather than the narrow `duration(_:)` a stat tile has room for, a trail match `RecordingStats.isCurrentTrailStale` has overtaken is hedged as "last on" rather than stated, and the finished-hike report reads its clock off the route's own end stamps rather than through `Hike.routeStatistics`, which walks every point on the calling thread — here, the main actor, inside an intent with a system execution budget. `AppShortcutsProvider` is capped at ten shortcuts and drops the rest in silence, which `OpenHikesShortcutsTests` guards.
- The Control Center toggle is the one intent declared in `OpenHikesShared`: the control extension has to compile its action type while the system still performs it in the app's process. It delegates through `HikeRecordingControlHandling`, whose app registration points back to the same `HikeIntentCoordinator`; the shared package never owns a second recording state. Its `StaticControlConfiguration` projects the App Group recording payload to start/stop, and `RecordingSharedStateStore` reloads that control alongside the widget timeline whenever the payload changes. The toggle is the one entry point that reads `HikeRecorder.phase` itself before delegating, so it settles automatic recovery first for the reason the rest of the coordinator does — and more sharply, since a Control Center tap is the likeliest of all to launch the process purely to perform an intent. It takes the same two foreground-only prompts as seriously as start and resume do: it reports `requiresForegroundAuthorization` when `HikeIntentAuthorization.needsForeground` holds, and the intent then `continueInForeground(_:)`s and calls back with `canPromptForLocation: true` — a re-run through `needsToContinueInForegroundError` would find the same unanswered authorization, because nothing between the two runs asked Core Location. This build proves App Intents metadata extraction from the shared package for both products, but it does not add or validate a `LiveActivityIntent`.
- Keep persisted identifiers stable: provider IDs, `SettingsKey` strings, `CloudSyncCoordinator.containerIdentifier`, `SharedStore.appGroupID`, widget kind, cache-key shape, and deep-link format are shared across launches, devices or targets. Update all entitlements/consumers together if an App Group or CloudKit container contract changes. CloudKit schema changes follow *Schema and migration policy*.
- Both unit-test bundles are hosted by the app, so it launches and runs its `.task`s before any test does. Startup work that writes shared state — today `OpenHikesView.restoreLastSelectedHike()`, which publishes a widget payload — must stay behind the `isRunningTests` guard, or it races the suites that assert on that state. The same guard is what keeps the test host from mirroring to the developer's real iCloud account, since it builds its own container at launch. UI tests run out-of-process and identify the app-under-test with `--ui-testing`. `Fixture.hike(in:configure:)` inserts before it runs `configure`, and must keep doing so: `Hike`'s device-local passthroughs are a silent no-op on a row with no `modelContext`.
- The app ships for iPhone, with a watchOS companion and nothing else. The phone targets declare `SUPPORTED_PLATFORMS = "iphoneos iphonesimulator"` and `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = 1`; an embedded extension's device family has to stay a subset of its host's, so `OpenWidget` moves with the app rather than independently. `OpenHikesWatch` is the exception and is a different kind of thing: `SUPPORTED_PLATFORMS = "watchos watchsimulator"`, `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = 4`, `WATCHOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 26.0`, and a `WKCompanionAppBundleIdentifier` naming the app. It is embedded through the app's *Embed Watch Content* phase and is a target dependency of it, which is what makes `xcodebuild build -scheme OpenHikes` compile it too — so the existing `builds` matrix and the archive job gate it without a job of their own, and there is no way to break the watch that leaves CI green. The `canImport(UIKit)`/`canImport(AppKit)` aliases and `#if os(iOS)` guards in the existing sources are kept — they cost nothing and are what a later iPad, Mac or visionOS target would be rebuilt from — but nothing verifies those paths compile any more, so treat them as unbuilt rather than supported. watchOS is not in that category: it builds on every run.
- A composite row is one accessibility element, not four. `HikeRow`, `StatFigure`, `StatRow`, `DetailRow` and the settings rows hide their decoration and expose a single label/value pair, so a UI test locates a row by its identifier plus a label prefix (`hikeRow(titled:)` in `UITestSupport.swift`) rather than by the `staticTexts` inside it. Selection that is drawn only as a tint or a checkmark also carries `.isSelected`; a glyph-only button carries its own `accessibilityLabel` and a `minimumTapTarget()`. Anything decorative is `.accessibilityHidden(true)`, and a `Text` that interpolates an SF Symbol needs a spoken label beside it. An identifier on a container is worse than none: SwiftUI pushes it down onto every descendant, so it both smothers the leaf identifiers underneath it and makes a whole section answer to one name — which is why the surface and difficulty sections carry theirs on the bar alone. `AccessibilityUITests` and `AccessibilityLabelUITests` are what enforce this.
- `OpenHikes/PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` is part of the shipping contract, not documentation. It declares four required-reason API codes — `CA92.1` for the app's own `UserDefaults`, `C617.1` and `3B52.1` for file timestamps inside the app's containers and through the document picker, and `35F9.1` for system uptime used as an elapsed-time measurement — plus `NSPrivacyTracking: false` and an empty tracking-domain array. An upload without it is rejected with ITMS-91053, and the rejection names the API rather than the manifest, so reaching for a new required-reason API means adding its code here in the same change. The collected-data array is **not** empty and has not been since Community shipped: publishing a hike sends a precise route, photographs, free text, the creator identifier moderation acts on, and the walk's timing — each declared linked, for app functionality, and not for tracking. `PrivacyManifestTests` reads the bundled manifest and pins that set, so a collected type added or dropped fails there rather than at an upload; App Store Connect's own privacy answers are separate and are not updated by the manifest. `OpenHikes/` is a file-system-synchronized group whose only membership exception is `Info.plist`, so the manifest is bundled with no `project.pbxproj` edit. Apple's authoritative code list is the DocC JSON behind `NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypeReasons`; the rendered HTML page is JavaScript-only and cannot be read by a fetch. `OpenWidgetExtension` deliberately carries **no** manifest of its own: it was audited and calls none of the required-reason APIs — `SharedStore` enumerates with `includingPropertiesForKeys: nil` and reads no timestamp, and the widget touches no `UserDefaults` and no uptime — so a manifest there would declare reasons the binary does not use. If a future upload rejection names the extension, that audit is what changed.
- `Info.plist` declares `NSSupportsLiveActivities`, without which `Activity.request` throws and nothing appears — the failure is silent from the hiker's side. `NSSupportsLiveActivitiesFrequentUpdates` is deliberately *absent*: this app updates on the hiker's own movement at a 20-second floor, which is well inside the ordinary budget, and asking for the frequent-update allowance would trade a battery warning in Settings for a rate nothing here wants. The hiker's own switch is `SettingsKey.liveActivitiesEnabled`, on by default; the system's per-app switch is read separately through `areActivitiesEnabled`, and both have to say yes.
- **Strings live in String Catalogs, and English is the only language.** `OpenHikes/`, `OpenWidget/`, `OpenHikesWatch/` and `OpenHikesWatchWidgets/` each carry a `Localizable.xcstrings` (#32) — one per target, because a target bundles only the catalog in its own folder, filled by extraction: every target builds with `SWIFT_EMIT_LOC_STRINGS = YES`, so SwiftUI `Text`/`Button`/`Label` literals, `accessibilityLabel`s and `String(localized:)` land in a `.stringsdata` per source file. Xcode's IDE folds those in on its own builds and `xcodebuild` does not, so after adding or changing user-facing text, build and run `Scripts/sync-string-catalogs.sh <derived-data>`; `--check` changes nothing and exits 2 when a catalog is behind the source. That script is the only completeness check there can be: an English key with no English entry is not compiled into the bundle at all — the key *is* the English — so no run-time lookup can tell a catalogued string from a missing one, and `StringCatalogTests` asserts only what the bundle does change. **A count is a plural variation in the catalog**, never an `if count == 1` at the call site (English has two forms, a translation may need four). A singular written out in words — "One photo has already been sent…" — is the `one` variation of the same key, and when the count drops out of it a later argument is named by position (`%2$@`), or it is handed the count. Every catalogued count is one now; the `count == 1` ternaries left are on plain `String`s (the GPX import button, the share disclosure, the community row, the field-metrics row, the Siri summary) and convert when those strings are catalogued. Figures are never catalogued: distances, heights and durations stay formatted per locale at the call site. What extraction does not reach, and is the remaining work before a second language ships: text that is a plain `String` until it is drawn (`Stat` labels, `MovementReminderWording`, error descriptions), and the shared package's presentation strings, which would need `defaultLocalization` and a catalog of its own. The App Store lists only English until a translation is complete.
- Never commit `OpenHikes/Secrets.plist`. Copy `Secrets.example.plist` locally for Stadia or Thunderforest keys; OpenStreetMap remains the keyless default.

## Schema and migration policy

The app currently has one installed device, its existing data is disposable, and the developer can reset local data and manage the CloudKit database. Preserve only the current formats. Do not add frozen historical models, `SchemaMigrationPlan` stages, launch-time data conversions, legacy decoding branches or fields retained solely for compatibility while these assumptions hold. This is a development reset policy, not a promise that an older store will open. Do not automatically erase stores on an open failure: the existing in-memory fallback and startup alert still handle corruption and I/O failures.

`OpenHikesSchema` is the single SwiftData schema, starting at version `1.0.0` for this fresh-store baseline and using the live `Hike`, `HikeWalk`, `TrailPoint`, `HikeLocalState` and `TrailDraftRecord` types. Both production and disk-backed test factories use it without a migration plan. Edit the live shape directly during this phase. This version starts a new baseline after discarding the previous stores; it neither reuses the historical V1 model nor downgrades an existing store or the CloudKit schema. Renumbering is acceptable only while previous stores are explicitly unsupported and reset. Old schemas and conversion implementations belong in git history. Keep current-format persistence tests that reopen both stores, verify the `hikeID` join and exercise deletion and recording recovery.

For an incompatible change, stop the app and widget and discard the affected local state before running the new build: both SwiftData stores and their SQLite side files/external storage, device-local tile manifests and files, recording journals, App Group snapshots/basemaps/pending fixes, or persisted settings as applicable. A clean reinstall plus clearing the shared App Group state is the simplest full reset. Coordinate any mirrored-data reset with the local reset so old cloud records cannot repopulate the fresh store. Clearing only the cloud database does not repair a local store, and clearing only local data can download the old cloud records again. This cleanup changes no mirrored fields and performs no live reset; pre-cleanup local stores and tile manifests are unsupported.

CloudKit still imposes its own constraints: non-optional mirrored attributes need inline defaults, relationships must be optional, and uniqueness constraints are forbidden. Keep the mirrored and unmirrored configurations separate: tile files, photo pixels and recording journals are still device-local, including after reinstalling or restoring cloud data on the same device. The tests in `MirroredCloudKitSchemaTests` check these constraints and compare the current mirrored fields against `MirroredCloudKitSchema.recordTypes`; they do not contact CloudKit.

CloudKit **records and schema are different**. The developer may clear disposable records, but resetting development restores the production schema if one exists; promoted record types and fields cannot simply be deleted, renamed or retyped. Use compatible additions or a new container if an incompatible production shape is unavoidable. Before a build uses the production environment, verify and deploy the current development schema in CloudKit Console, including every mirrored record type and field (`CD_Hike`, `CD_HikeWalk`, `CD_TrailPoint` and their `CD_` fields). Production **is** deployed, and has been read rather than assumed: the Community section below records the shape the 2026-09-13 exports found, which is now development's field for field. Record verified deployment/reset facts here, not in runtime code or a date-parsing test. Apple's [model constraints](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/coredata/creating-a-core-data-model-for-cloudkit) and [schema deployment guidance](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/cloudkit/deploying-an-icloud-container-s-schema) own the platform rules.

The app and widget keep explicit current-format versions for their shared snapshots (currently v1). A version is required and only an exact match is read; missing, older, newer and malformed versions are refused with diagnostics. There is no unversioned-v0 fallback or rewrite-on-save upgrade. Keep this format check and the journal header/version check: rejecting unreadable bytes is ordinary validation, not a migration. Optional fields remain optional when absence has a current meaning, such as no walk, no elevation or no custom name. Derived caches can be regenerated when their current shape fails to decode.

Tile keys contain provider/zoom/x/y only. No provider substitutes display scale into its URL, so the former scale suffix split identical tiles between renderer and downloader. The scale suffix converter, file renamer and unused `OfflineDownloadRecord.scale` are removed; reset old tile state instead. Weather readings require their explicit subject kind. Do not retain old payload acceptance tests as current requirements. Recording flag bit 1 is unused; the current bit values remain unchanged without carrying retired-journal compatibility tests.

Revisit this policy only when installs or data must survive upgrades. At that point, freeze the actual then-current model and every encoded value type before changing it, introduce a real versioned migration plan, and test on-disk previous-version stores through both configurations. Recover historical shapes from git if they truly need support; never invent a previous schema by putting a new version number on today's model. Keep any future migration rationale, reset procedure and CloudKit deployment notes in this section rather than scattering them through source headers, README or separate migration documents.

## Render isolation, in practice

The claim these rules protect is measured rather than asserted: an idle app with a map on screen evaluates zero SwiftUI bodies and costs 0.6% of one core, a sustained chart scrub moves the map seventeen times without re-evaluating any body above the chart, and a backgrounded recording renders nothing at all. A run's own report carries the figures. Five rules below each produced a convincing wrong answer first, and are worth knowing before changing anything on the render path.

**Only a `View` type is a boundary.** A helper `func`, a computed `var`, and a `.toolbar`/`.safeAreaInset`/`.overlay` closure are all inlined into the body that declares them, so an observable read inside one registers as an input of *that* body. This is how a tick mark came to rebuild a whole photo grid: the selection lived correctly in an `@Observable` controller, and the cells were built by a `private func cell(_:at:)` in the sheet's scope. If a body is re-running and the observable read is not visible in it, look for those four before looking anywhere else.

**State can be correctly owned and incorrectly placed.** `@State` invalidates its declaring view whether or not `body` reads it — a navigation path held as `@State` on the root re-rendered the entire map screen underneath a full-screen cover that completely obscured it, and an `.onChange` writing a `@State` that no body ever read still cost two body evaluations. `SheetPresentation` is the fix shape: a stable `@Observable` holding the raw state as `@ObservationIgnored` storage and publishing only coarser derived flags, so pushing a photo onto a hike — the same screen at the same height — flips nothing at all.

**`@Environment(\.dismiss)` is the dynamic property that invalidates most.** The rule above is not about `@State` in particular: *any* `DynamicProperty` invalidates its declaring view whether or not `body` reads it, and `DismissAction` is the one that changes constantly. SwiftUI hands out a fresh, non-equatable one on every pass through the presentation machinery, and a single scene-phase transition drives several — so `Button("Done") { dismiss() }` written into a screen's own `.toolbar` re-renders that whole screen every time the app leaves or re-enters the foreground, for a value nothing on screen depends on. Measured on the `photo-discovery` scenario: one backgrounding rebuilt the twelve-cell review grid, its toolbar and every cell's accessibility label **eight** times across ~300 ms, and SwiftUI's own `_logChanges()` named `_dismiss` as the only changed property in seven of the eight. The same shape cost `HikePhotoViewer` seven passes of a screen that re-sorts the gallery on each, and `SettingsView` six of a seven-section `Form`. `DismissButton` and `.dismiss(when:)` in `General/Dismissal.swift` are the fix shape, and they work because a `ViewModifier` is a boundary for the same reason a `View` is: its dynamic properties are its own, and its `body(content:)` re-wraps a subtree the parent has already built. No screen should declare `@Environment(\.dismiss)` when the only thing that closes it is a button or a condition.

**A computed property that sorts looks like a field access.** `Hike.orderedPhotos` was read six times in one body pass of the photo viewer for that reason. Its comparator also allocated: comparing `(capturedAt, id.uuidString)` tuples makes Swift build both sides before comparing, so every comparison allocated two 36-character strings rather than only the ties the tie-break exists for.

**Not every well-argued prediction survives a measurement.** `SettingsView`'s unbounded `@Query` was predicted to charge all seven `Form` sections for every write to any `Hike`. Measured, it was 2.0 body evaluations either way, because SwiftData coalesces the writes into one invalidation the explicit state changes already paid for. A prediction about SwiftUI cost is a hypothesis; measure both sides.

**A same-value write is filtered by `@Observable`, not by SwiftData — and only when the type is `Equatable`.** Measured across `String`, `Double`, `Bool`, `Date`, `UUID`, `String?`, dictionaries, an `@Attribute(.externalStorage)` array and a to-many relationship: a `@Model` notifies on **every** write, equal or not, inserted into a context or not, and does so per-property. A plain `@Observable` storing an `Equatable` value notifies on **none** of them; storing a non-`Equatable` one — `CLLocationCoordinate2D` — notifies on all. The filtering lives in `@Observable`'s macro expansion. Three consequences. A dedup guard on an `Equatable` `@Observable` property (`RouteStyle.apply`, `SheetPresentation.pathDidChange`) is belt-and-braces over undocumented runtime behaviour and **cannot be protected by a zero-assertion test** — delete it and the test stays green, because the runtime already filtered the write. A dedup guard on a non-`Equatable` one (`RouteHighlight.move(to:)`, `LocationManager.publish`) is load-bearing app code and its test really does go red. And a test asserting a zero *upstream* of an `@Observable` needs an explicit precondition that the write it is filtering actually happened, or it measures nothing. `OpenHikesTests/Map/RenderIsolationTests+Observation.swift` pins both runtime behaviours; those pins are the tripwire if either changes, and they are the one thing in that family that cannot be mutation-verified, since a runtime change cannot be induced.

**A zero-assertion is only evidence if you have watched it go red.** Around thirty in the render-isolation family were audited by deleting the behaviour each claimed to hold; two were decorative for the reason above, and one hole was real and unrelated — `LocationManager.minimumPublishInterval` could be deleted entirely with the whole suite still green, because `ObservationCounter` re-arms through a `Task` and so sees ten writes in one runloop turn exactly once either way. An observation count cannot measure a throttle; assert the throttle's observable effect instead.

The rules above are the standing ones, and each was measured once. What can measure them again is `Self._logChanges()` in the body under suspicion, which makes SwiftUI name the inputs that differed, and Instruments — a Time Profiler trace for a body that is costing frames, Energy Log and Location Energy Impact for what a recording costs a battery on a device.

## Field metrics from real devices

`General/Diagnostics/FieldMetrics/` is what is left of the diagnostics side, and note it is *not* `#if DEBUG` — unlike everything else in `Diagnostics/` — because MetricKit only delivers against Release builds in the field. It is split along one line: `FieldMetricsDigest.swift` holds every judgement the app makes about a payload and imports no MetricKit at all, which is the only reason `FieldMetricsDigestTests` can exist, since `MXMetricPayload` has no initializer and cannot be synthesised. Only four `mxSignpost` spans exist, deliberately: Apple limits how many the system processes and the failure mode is silent, so a fifth span does not error, it costs the other four their data. `FieldSignpost.Span` is `CaseIterable` and its count is asserted, so a fifth has to be added on purpose.

## Energy policies in force

Five policies decide what the app spends. Each was a measured finding once and each is now shipping behaviour, with the full argument in the source header so the rationale cannot drift away from the code it justifies. Do not weaken one without a measurement.

- **GPS accuracy is a function of conditions**, not a constant (`Recording/RecordingEnergyPolicy.swift`). `desiredAccuracy` drops only for Low Power Mode or thermal `.serious` and above; `distanceFilter` widens for those and for standing still, taking the larger candidate. `.fair` thermal is deliberately excluded — a phone in a sunlit jacket pocket sits there all summer, and a mitigation that is always on is indistinguishable from having lowered the default. `PowerStateMonitor` watches both notifications, so the transition with no fix to prompt it — a hiker stopping for lunch as the battery crosses 20% — still reconfigures.
- **Tile fetching is split by purpose**, not by caller (`Tiles/TileNetworkPolicy.swift`). What matters is whether anyone is waiting for the tile: `loadTile` takes the purpose and defaults to `.interactive`, while `saveTileDurably` fixes it at `.speculative`. Cellular allows interactive and denies speculative; offline and Low Data Mode deny both; Low Power Mode and thermal pressure deny only speculative. The asymmetry is the point — a hiker looking at the map gets their tile, and what stops is the app spending a metered radio on tiles nobody asked to see. None of it is configurable, because a switch is a question the hiker has to answer correctly *before* the walk to get the right behaviour during it. Every refusal carries a short, stable `reason` down to `TileCache.withheldFetch(forKey:reason:hasStaleCoverage:token:otherwise:)`, which logs it and serves saved coverage where there is any; a tile that silently never loads is the hardest thing in this pipeline to debug, and this policy creates that situation on purpose.
- **A pause spends nothing unless something will read it** (`Reminders/MovementReminderController.swift`, `RecordingLocationSource.startMovementWatch()`). `HikeRecorder.pause()` used to stop the GPS outright; it now asks the reminder controller whether the pause is worth watching and stops it outright whenever the answer is no — reminders switched off, or a pause taken before the first fix, which leaves no anchor to measure a departure from. When the answer is yes the watch is the *cheapest delivery that can still notice a departure*, and which one that is depends on authorization rather than on a setting: Always gets significant-location-change monitoring, which needs neither the background mode nor the activity session, so the continuous feed, the session and the status indicator all go for the length of the pause; When In Use keeps the feed at `RecordingEnergyProfile.pausedWatch` (hundred-metre accuracy, hundred-metre filter), because an app that stops updating location is suspended and a suspended app notices nothing at all. A paused *walk* along a followed trail is watched by the matched fixes its feeds were already delivering and costs nothing new — which also means it is silent for a hiker whose phone is in a pocket with background tracking off, and the settings footer gives that case its own sentence — a paused walk is watched while the app is open, and behind it only with Background Trail Tracking on — rather than letting the recording's “without Always access” clause stand for both and promising a reminder the app cannot send.
- **The display is held only on a claim, and only if asked** (`General/ScreenWake.swift`). `isIdleTimerDisabled` was never set, which is right for a six-hour walk in a pocket and wrong for a hiker standing at a junction while the screen dims every thirty seconds — each of those wakes pays a display ramp and a render, repeatedly, so the cheap default is the expensive one in exactly the case it was meant to help. So it is a switch, `SettingsKey.keepScreenAwake`, **off** by default, and three answers have to agree before anything is held: the switch, a *live* subject (a recording session that exists, or a walk under way), and `scenePhase == .active`. It is scoped to the two screens where the question arises — `RecordingView` and `HikeDetailView` — through `.keepsScreenAwake(while:)`, so a Settings screen left open in a pocket holds nothing. `ScreenWakeCoordinator` counts claims rather than storing a flag, because a navigation transition presents the incoming screen before the outgoing one disappears and a flag would be cleared by the screen that was leaving; it is also the one place `UIApplication.isIdleTimerDisabled` is written, behind an injectable seam, since both unit bundles are hosted by the app.
- **A backgrounded recording draws nothing and ticks nothing.** `MapView.Coordinator` gates the overlay apply on foreground, observed through `UIApplication` lifecycle notifications rather than `scenePhase` so it stays entirely off SwiftUI's render path; the `withObservationTracking` registration continues regardless, since the revision must keep being tracked, and the work is deferred rather than dropped and caught up in one pass on return. The recording card's duration figure builds its 1 Hz `TimelineView` only while `scenePhase` is `.active` — that one *is* on the render path, deliberately, because the question is whether the `TimelineView` is in the hierarchy at all and only SwiftUI can answer it. Do not assume iOS suspends that timer: a suspended app runs no timers, but this app holds the location background mode for the entire hike, which is exactly what keeps it running.

## The community feature

Sharing a hike publishes it to the **public** CloudKit database of the same container the mirrored store uses. That is a different database with a different owner: public storage is the developer's, private storage is the hiker's own iCloud quota. The distinction is what makes this feature possible at all without contradicting *Photo pixels stay on the device the photo was added on* below — that decision is about the private database and still holds.

**Every submission is reviewed by a person, and the gate is the schema rather than a flag.** CloudKit grants permissions per *record type*, never per field or per record. A single type with a `moderationState` field therefore cannot express this: whoever may write a submission may write whatever they like into their own state field. So there are two types, and `CommunitySchema` is the one place they are spelled:

- `CommunityHikeSubmission` — what a hiker uploads. `_world` read, `_icloud` create, `_creator` **read only**. Anybody may make one; nobody but the reviewer may change one.
- `CommunityHike` — the published listing, carrying a reference to a submission plus the denormalised fields a query needs. `_world` read, and create *and write* granted to a custom admin role and to nobody else. One of those fields is `authorID`, the submission's creator, which the reviewer copies across from the submission's *Created By* when they publish — see *Blocking is device-local* below for what it is for and why a listing without it is dropped.

- `CommunitySubmissionNotice` — one record per submission, carrying a reference to it and nothing else. `_icloud` create, and read *and* write granted to the `reviewer` role and to nobody else. It is the queue, and it exists because a CloudKit index belongs to a type rather than to a role: there is no way to make submissions listable for a reviewer without making them listable for everybody, so the thing that gets listed is a separate type that only a reviewer may read.

**Publishing is done in the app, from the *Community* tab, and the gate is the grant rather than the absence of a method.** It used to be one `CommunityHike` record created by hand in the Console, which is what let review ship before any review tooling did. The correction is worth keeping written down because the old shape reads as the safer one: what stops an ordinary hiker publishing is `GRANT CREATE, WRITE TO reviewer`, enforced by the server against whoever is calling. A modified client may call `CommunityTransporting.publish(_:)`; it gets a permission failure, as it would for the request it could always have hand-rolled. Leaving the method out protected nothing — it only meant the one person allowed to publish had to copy `authorID` across by eye, and a hike was silently invisible when they got it wrong. `CommunityReviewQueue` holds what is waiting, `CommunityReviewView` is where one is looked at and published or declined, and `CommunityPendingSubmission` is the queue entry — which carries the listing's fields so that *what the reviewer saw is what gets published*, rather than re-reading the submission after the decision. **A reviewer may correct two things and no others: the title, and which photographs go.** Both exist because the alternative to each was declining, which deletes a hiker's whole upload and never tells them — so a good walk called "Morning walk", or one with a single photograph that cannot be published, used to cost the hike. They are unalike in where they land, and that difference is the whole design: the title is written onto `CommunityPendingSubmission` before `publish(_:)` and reaches the **listing** only, because nothing reads a submission's title after publication, so the hiker's own words survive untouched on the record; a photograph has no such trick and comes off the submission itself, see *A submission is write-once* below. The description, the route and the credit are not editable by anybody, which keeps *correction* and *authorship* on opposite sides of a line. `docs/terms/` and `docs/privacy/` both describe these two, and must keep describing whatever this list becomes.

**The review section is invisible to everybody who is not a reviewer, and nothing on the device decides that.** There is no role flag, no cached answer and no permission check anywhere in the app: `pendingSubmissions()` asks the server, a permission failure comes back as an empty list rather than an error, and a section with no rows is not drawn. A build with the section forced open gets an empty section. The queue is asked for once per launch behind the same tab selection that opts into browsing — every launch runs this query, and almost every one of them is somebody with no queue — and a **failed** load draws nothing rather than a row, which is the one deliberate silence in the feature: a *couldn't load the review queue* row in a valley would be an error about a feature almost nobody has. Failures of the *actions* are the opposite and are reported on the screen that asked.

**A submission is write-once, and that is what makes review mean anything.** The listing points at the submission rather than at a copy of its contents, so an author who kept write access could swap the route, the description or the photo assets of an already-approved submission and have `detail(for:)` serve the replacement under the approved listing, unreviewed. Hence no write permission outside the admin role — which also means the app cannot withdraw or amend a submission: sharing an amended hike makes a new one, and a takedown is a reviewer's delete. What the app can do, and now does, is *ask* for one. `CommunityWithdrawal` composes the email `docs/privacy/` and `docs/terms/` have promised all along, and the reason it had to exist is the mechanism above rather than the affordance: a delete needs a record ID, the submission and listing names live only on the `Hike` row, and deleting the hike is precisely what destroys the one thing "enough detail to identify it" could mean. So the request is composed *before* the gesture that would make it unanswerable. It claims nothing about whether a takedown happened, for the same reason the share sheet claims nothing about publication. **The one exception is a reviewer removing individual photographs, and it is an exception to the mechanism rather than to the reasoning.** `CommunityTransporting.keepOnlyPhotos(_:of:staging:)` rewrites the two photo fields under `GRANT WRITE TO reviewer` — the grant declining already needs — and it runs **before** the listing is created, so nothing is serving the record while it changes and what a reviewer approved is still what everybody downloads. It exists because the listing carries a photo *count* and the pictures are assets on the record it names: a photograph hidden from a listing stays fetchable by anyone who opens the hike, so hiding is not removing. CloudKit cannot drop one element of an asset field, so the kept photographs are re-uploaded from the copies the review screen downloaded; the save is `.changedKeys` against a record fetched with one text field, which is what keeps the route asset and the text off the wire and unwritten. `CommunityHikeDetail.hasEveryPhoto` gates the whole affordance — a rewrite built from a partial download would delete the photograph that did not arrive. `_world` reads the type for the other half of the same fetch: a reference being readable does not make its target readable, and browsing is account-free, so without it a signed-out hiker could find a hike and not open it. The cost, stated plainly: an unreviewed submission is readable by anyone holding its record name — unguessable, and not enumerable, but a name rather than a permission. The alternative, copying every approved route and photograph into an admin-only record, cannot be done by hand in the Console for a dozen assets and would make review wait on tooling that does not exist yet.

**Indexes are not created by a first save, and a query against an unindexed field fails at runtime.** On `CommunityHike` the Console needs `location` QUERYABLE *and* SORTABLE (the predicate filters on it and the results sort by distance from the same point), `title` SEARCHABLE (the typed query is a full-text `self contains`, because CloudKit's `BEGINSWITH` is case-sensitive and anchored), and `publishedAt` SORTABLE. `authorID` needs **no index**: blocking is applied on the device, so the field is read off rows that have already arrived and is never a predicate — indexing it would let anybody enumerate one person's published hikes. On `CommunityHikeSubmission`, **no index at all** — including the `___recordID` QUERYABLE the Console adds by default, which has to be removed. `CommunitySubmissionNotice` is the exception that proves the rule and needs two: `___recordID` QUERYABLE, without which the queue cannot be listed at all, and `___createTime` SORTABLE, so the oldest is reviewed first and no client-written date can jump the queue. Indexing it leaks nothing because only the `reviewer` role may read it — permission is doing the work an absent index does one type over. `routeOutline`, added to that type for the map's lines, is no exception and needs none: it is read by a fetch of record IDs with `desiredKeys`, which is a fetch and not a query. That absence is the security control that keeps a world-readable pending submission from being enumerable: the type is only ever *fetched by record ID*, which needs no index, and adding one would list every unreviewed upload to anybody. **Deployed to the development environment on 2026-09-12 and verified there**, with `xcrun cktool import-schema` rather than by hand in the Console — export the schema, edit that file, import it back, because the import is declarative and whole-file. `CommunityHikeSubmission.routeOutline` postdates that import and **reached development on its own, carrying `QUERYABLE SEARCHABLE SORTABLE`** — the auto-created defaults the paragraph below warns about, and the enumeration leak this whole rule exists to refuse. Another `import-schema` stripped all three (#272), and the 2026-09-13 development export shows the type carrying no index at all, `___recordID` included. That is the warning demonstrating itself within a day of being written, so read it as a standing instruction rather than a historical note: **re-export after every change and look at the index list, because the field you just added is indexed**. The custom role is called `reviewer` and was created by `CREATE ROLE reviewer;` in the same file; no Console step was needed for it. Two things the live container taught: a type CloudKit auto-creates from a first save arrives with `GRANT WRITE TO "_creator"` and every field QUERYABLE, SEARCHABLE and SORTABLE, which is how `CommunityHikeSubmission` first existed here — pending submissions were enumerable in practice, not in theory, until the import above replaced it; and a field added to `CommunitySchema` later will reach the database with those same defaults, so re-export and re-check after any change rather than assuming this shape held. **Production is deployed, and now matches development field for field.** `cktool` has no promote subcommand and cannot even validate against production (`endpoint not applicable in the environment 'production'`), so the promote stays a Console button and the only way to read production is `export-schema --environment production`. Do that before believing anything in this paragraph. The 2026-09-13 promote settled the question this paragraph used to end on, so record the answer rather than the doubt: **a promote can drop an index and downgrade a `GRANT`, not only add.** Production's `CommunityHikeSubmission` went from the auto-created shape — every field QUERYABLE, SEARCHABLE and SORTABLE, `GRANT WRITE TO "_creator"` — to no index at all, `___recordID` included, and `GRANT READ`. Both halves of the schema's reason for existing therefore hold in production: an author cannot rewrite their own approved submission, and pending submissions are not enumerable. The four-field `CD_Hike` gap that used to block the press — `author`, `importedAuthorName`, `keywords` and `trackDescription`, all four stored `String?` on the model and none ever exported with a non-nil value, so SwiftData had never created the columns — was closed the same day, by getting a non-nil value for each into development and promoting again. Both environments exported byte-identical after that promote (`md5 78ab709e335764d778873efd1ccbdaa3`); the schema has moved on twice since, and the current pair of numbers is at the end of the Community section below. Note why `MirroredCloudKitSchemaTests` did not catch that gap, because the reason outlives the gap: it compares two local descriptions and never reads a live database, so a field the model declares and the container lacks passes it. The live check is an export, and it is the only one there is.

**The list has two sources, and only one file knows it.** Most of what the *Community* tab shows is not published by anybody: `MergedCommunityTransport` is a `CommunityTransporting` holding the CloudKit one and a `CuratedTrailSourcing`, so `CommunityBrowser` — 1,025 lines, already parameterised on a two-case question with two task handles and two accept branches — learns nothing. Three rules hold it up and each is a correction to the obvious version. **A published hike never loses its place**: the `limit` is spent on CloudKit first and only the remainder is asked of Overpass, because asking both for a full page and truncating would push real people's hikes off the bottom as soon as an area had twenty-five waymarked routes in it, which in the Alps is most areas. **One source failing is not the answer failing**: `state` describes the nearby request as a whole and a `.failed` draws *These are the hikes from the last search that worked* over everything, so each half is caught separately and only both failing throws — and then the CloudKit failure is the one reported. A curated failure is instead carried back beside the rows as a `CuratedTrailOutage` on `CommunityNearbyAnswer` and drawn as a caption under *Search this area*, because catching it and only logging it left a rate-limited hiker unable to tell a busy Overpass from an area with no waymarked routes in it; the button stays **enabled**, since the published half is still askable and it is the one control that tab has. **A curated id never reaches CloudKit**: every per-listing method routes on `CommunityIdentity`, and `takeDown(_:)` refuses a curated listing rather than forwarding it, since it builds `CKRecord.ID`s out of the listing's two names and deletes them.

**`CommunityOrigin` is a sum type because the alternative was a sentinel, and the sentinel was load-bearing.** A curated route has no author and no submission, and those are not merely unused fields — `CommunityBlockList.block(_:at:)` refuses an empty author id and says why (blocking on one would hide every *other* listing missing it), and `CloudKitCommunityTransport` builds a `CKRecord.ID` straight out of a submission id. So the two live inside `.published(submissionID:authorID:)` and the compiler is what keeps them apart; `.openStreetMap(relationID:facts:)` carries the OSM facts in the case for the same reason. `hikeDate` became `Date?` in the same change, because the `.distantPast` that used to stand in for a missing one rendered as *1 January 1*. **Report, Block and Take Down are therefore absent for a curated route, not disabled.** Both halves of Guideline 1.2 are about user-generated content and an OSM relation is not that: there is nobody to block — the old fallback title read *Block This Hiker* about nobody — and no record for a reviewer to delete. What replaces them is a link to the relation on openstreetmap.org, which is also the ODbL attribution `TileAttribution` already requires be *linked* rather than merely present.

**Only *Search this area* asks Overpass** — both of them. The *Community* tab's pill asks for waymarked routes and the trail maker's, which is a second instance of the same `MapAreaSearchView`, asks what is on the ground near the line being drawn; the rate-limit gate and the one retry a busy answer gets are `OverpassConversation`'s and are held by both sources rather than written twice. `CommunityNearbyScope` is a parameter on the nearby question — `.publishedOnly` or `.withCuratedTrails` — rather than a setting on the transport, which is a value every caller shares and two in-flight requests could disagree about. Opening the *Community* tab, refilling the list after a block and the deferred first-region opt-in are all published-only; the pill's tap and the *Try Again* that stands in for it are the two that ask for both. It used to be every nearby request, so a hiker who never touched the button could still spend two Overpass round trips per pan-and-confirm against an API that allows a handful of slots per address. The scope is also carried through `CommunityBrowser.accept`: a published-only answer reports `nil` for the curated half because it never asked, and writing that through would clear a rate-limit caption that still stands.

**Curated routes are kept on disk, and a refused search draws them.** `CuratedTrailStore` writes one JSON file per relation under `Caches/CuratedTrails` — thirty days, 200 files, evicted least-recently-used with a read re-stamping the file — so a relation is downloaded once rather than once a launch, and reads go memory, then disk, then Overpass. The memory cache in `CuratedTrailSource` stays in front of it: it is what keeps a browse off the file system on every pin, and it is the only one that holds `.absent`, which is deliberately never written down (the fix for a route too fragmented to assemble is somebody editing OSM, and a file saying *nothing here* would outlast the edit). When the listing pass is refused, `MergedCommunityTransport` falls back to the stored routes whose pin stands in the searched area — **and keeps the outage**, because nothing records which areas have been listed, so those rows are what happens to be on the device rather than an answer. The alternative considered and rejected was a coverage index: it is the coherence problem the memory-only version was right to refuse, and the one question it would answer quickly is asked only when a round trip was not going to arrive anyway.

**Two Overpass passes, and the bounding box is the day-hike filter.** Measured against the live API over one Berchtesgaden search box: `out geom` returned **7.0 MB** for 105 relations — 121,496 points — and `out tags bb` returned **43.7 KB** carrying every tag *plus* a box per relation. So the list is built from the cheap pass and lines are fetched by id for the routes that survive. That filter is the part worth keeping written down, because `route=hiking` relations are **not day hikes**: the same box held routes of 57, 170, 237, 411 and 531 km. The `distance` tag cannot do the filtering — it is on **2%** of them, and one measured value was the string `"4.6 km"` — but the box can, and a 20 km diagonal ceiling keeps 97 of 102 whose true lengths run 0.1–30.7 km while rejecting exactly those five. `CuratedTrailQuery.maximumRadiusMeters` is 40 km because the listing pass scales with the *area* of the box, and `CommunityQueryPolicy.maximumRadiusMeters` **is** that figure rather than a second one of its own.

**A relation is a bag of ways, not a path, and member order is not usable.** Taking the members in the order Overpass returns them and joining each to the previous produces one connected line for **46** of 97 day-hike relations; matching endpoints across the whole set produces one for **74**, and for most of the rest the largest connected run is already 95% of the route. The matching is *exact* at seven decimal places rather than distance-based, and that is the right test rather than an approximation of one: ways in a relation **share OSM nodes**, and Overpass emits a shared node's coordinate identically on both — a 30 m tolerance assembles 75 against exact matching's 74, for a dictionary lookup instead of a scan. What survives is the longest run and nothing else, because `CommunityRouteLine` is one polyline and three disconnected runs drawn as one puts a straight stroke across a valley the path does not cross. The distance on the row is then measured from exactly the line that is drawn, which is the rule `CommunityImport` already states. Relations too fragmented for that are **dropped rather than shown short** (`minimumConnectedShare`, 0.6, costs six of 97): a third of the Almbachklamm under the Almbachklamm's name, with its waymark and its two ends beside it, is a quieter kind of wrong than showing nothing.

**A curated route has no photographs and no elevation, and only one of the two already degraded correctly.** Measured: **zero** `image` tags on 106 relations, and zero `ele` on 1,725 geometry nodes. `photoCount: 0` drops the photo clause from the row's subtitle and skips the strip, which is the existing behaviour and is right. The chart was not: `RouteCoordinate.elevation` is already `Double?`, so every curated trail took the *No elevation data* card — turning a rare admission about one person's upload into a permanent grey placeholder on most of the screens this feature opens, sitting where a hiker looks first and saying only that there is nothing to look at. `CommunityHikeView.elevationSection` draws **nothing at all** when there are no heights, which is the rule every other section on that screen already follows — and there are heights now, from somewhere else. **Stadia Maps answers the question OpenStreetMap cannot**: `CuratedElevationSourcing` is asked once, on `MergedCommunityTransport.detail(for:)`, for a route sampled down to 200 evenly spaced points (a height every hundred metres on the longest route `CuratedTrailQuery` allows, and finer below that), and the heights land back on exactly those points so the profile is a coarse *reading* rather than a fine-looking interpolation. One vendor rather than a second one: the key, the terms, the URL redaction and the privacy paragraph all already exist for the paid map styles. It is asked **on open and never for a list** — a page offers twenty-five routes to draw one — which is the rule `HikeTrailAnalysis` already follows on that screen, and **only for an OpenHikes Pro subscriber**: every call is billed against the key that already sits behind the paid map styles, so `StadiaElevationSource` reads `MapEntitlement.current` *before* it forms a request and refuses with `.notEntitled` otherwise. `.unknown` refuses too — the same *not yet* `MapEntitlementState.tapAction(for:)` turns into `.wait` — so the first second of a launch spends nothing on a question StoreKit has not answered. A refusal, a timeout, a build with no key or a hiker without the subscription all leave the route exactly as it came and open the hike without a chart, which is what the screen did before heights existed. The composite's `elevation` defaults to `DormantElevationSource`, so a caller that has not thought about it cannot spend a billable call or reach a vendor from a suite; `makeCommunityTransport()` is the one place that opts in, and `SeededElevationSource` is what `--ui-test-community=curated` gets. The chart carries a credit line naming Stadia, drawn only for a curated listing and only when a chart is: a published hike's heights are the ones the hiker who walked it uploaded. A hike in the library keeps its placeholder — `HikeElevationPlaceholder` — because *no elevation data in this file* tells the hiker something true about a thing they chose to import. What a curated route has *instead* is what no hiker's upload carries: a waymark (`osmc:symbol` ~100% of named relations), whether it is a loop (`roundtrip`, or derived from the line's two ends), and where it runs between (`from`/`to`/`via`, ~59% in the Alps and ~88% in the UK). It also gets `TrailSurfaceSection` and `TrailDifficultySection` for free, because `CommunityHikeView` already runs `HikeTrailAnalysis` on open — and more accurately than for a recorded hike, since its route *is* the trail geometry.

**The test rule is unchanged and now covers both sources.** `makeCommunityTransport()` still returns `nil` for every launch running tests, so the picker stays absent; the two halves are behind **one** guard rather than two. Overpass is the safer of the pair — a read against a public API, where CloudKit is a write into a database every user can see — but the rule is that a suite reaches no network, and a volunteer-run service is the last one to make an exception for. `--ui-test-community=curated` selects `SeededCommunityTransport` plus `SeededCuratedTrailSource`, which is the only way automation reaches a *mixed* list, and the mixed list is what the shipping app draws: everything the two row kinds differ in — the glyph, the subtitle's parts, the absent menu items — is invisible unless both are on screen at once. `CommunityCuratedUITests` is the class that spends it, and it is the one that has to exist for that argument to mean anything: a run against `.seeded` sees a list where every row has an author, every menu has three items, and nothing on the page mentions OpenStreetMap, so it passes in full while the curated half is broken in any way at all. It asserts the merge (both halves in one list, the published rows still there), the row's subtitle in words rather than by its glyph — which is `accessibilityHidden` like every other decoration in that row — the conditional ODbL credit in both directions, and Report and Block being **absent** on a curated route while present on a published one in the same launch. Like the rest of the functional UI automation it runs from `Scripts/run-ui-tests.sh` and not in CI.

**The map's results and the typed query's are separate lists.** `CommunityBrowser` keeps `nearbyListings` and `matchingListings` apart, with one in-flight task each, because they answer different questions and are drawn in different places — the *Community* tab's list (and, while typing, a *Near Here* section under the matches) and the *Community Hikes* search section.
