While they shared one array a pan past the policy's threshold overwrote a typed search's results, and clearing the field left title matches standing wherever the zoom ceiling refused the replacement query. `state` describes the nearby request alone; a failed title search is logged and touches neither it nor the remembered region. The search field coalesces title edits through a cancellable `.task(id:)` and a 300 ms clock wait, keyed by the trimmed, lowercased query. Edits cancel the old title response synchronously; clearing also drops matches immediately, and Return submits the pending query without waiting or asking twice. That deduplication is about reusing an *answer*, so a failed title search forgets the word it asked and Return can ask it again — nothing on screen reports a failed title search, which makes resubmitting the only retry there is. This bounds requests during typing; no battery saving has been measured.

**The map offers, and the hiker asks.** `distanceToLocation:` resolves at around ten kilometres, so a request per pan spends the shared public-database quota redrawing an identical list. `CommunityQueryPolicy` therefore refuses unless the centre moved more than **half** the last radius or the zoom changed by more than a factor of two, and answers `.tooFarOut` above `CuratedTrailQuery.maximumRadiusMeters`, where a result means "somewhere on this continent". Both figures are now set by Overpass rather than by CloudKit, because an accepted offer spends a listing pass against a volunteer-run API where CloudKit's `distanceToLocation:` merely cannot tell the difference. **There is one ceiling and it is the curated one**: there used to be two — 150 km here, 40 km there — with a band between them where the pill was enabled, a tap spent a CloudKit query, and the curated half answered `[]` with no failure to report, so a hiker looking at 100 km of map got no trails and nothing saying that zooming in was the answer. Raising the pan threshold costs the hiker nothing, which is what makes it affordable: the pill is permanent, so a tap with no offer standing still re-asks through `retry()` — a refused offer withholds the invitation, never the ability. What it returns is an **offer** rather than a search: `action(for:)` is side-effect free — a pan is a run of settles and the second must not withdraw what the first raised — `CommunityBrowser.areaPrompt` is what the map draws as *Search this area*, and `commit(_:)` records the area only when the hiker takes it. That is both cheaper than the automatic re-query it replaced (a pan nobody confirms costs nothing) and the only version of this that is legible: the list used to replace itself under the hiker's thumb for reasons nothing on screen gave. `CommunityAreaName` then heads the list with the place MapKit calls that area, so *Nearby* is a description rather than a control. Browsing is still opt-in — until the *Community* tab is selected nothing reaches the network, geocoder included — and that one selection is the single request nobody confirms twice. The region reaches `CommunityBrowser` from `MapView.Coordinator`'s `regionDidChangeAnimated` and is stored `@ObservationIgnored`, so no SwiftUI body reads it.

**The shared hikes are the second of the sheet's two lists, and they are on the map.** `MapSheetList` is the segmented control above them — *My Hikes* and *Community* — and it is bound to `CommunityBrowser.isBrowsing` rather than to state of its own, because the tab and the browse session are the same thing: selecting *Community* is the opt-in, leaving it is `stopBrowsing()`, and a second flag could only disagree with the first about which list is showing. That replaced a *Community Hikes* section under the hiker's own hikes, which had in turn replaced the *Nearby* chip. The chip's sin was being an unlabelled mode — the same records under two headings depending on how they were found, and no way to see one half without giving up the other; the section fixed that and buried the shared half under a library that only ever gets longer. A picker labelled on both sides is not the chip: nothing is a mode you can be in without being told, and neither list carries a title of its own because the picker is the title. The *Hide* button is gone with the section; the other segment is the off switch. The results are also drawn as `MKMarkerAnnotationView`s through `MapCommunityAnnotations`, which closes the loop the feature was missing: the region is the query and, until then, its answer existed only as rows in a sheet drawn over the map that asked. The pins are observed off `nearbyListings` by the coordinator and a callout's accessory opens the same preview a row does, through `CommunityBrowser.onOpenListing` — set by `OpenHikesView`, because MapKit draws the pins and the destination is a push into a stack the map cannot see. The pill stands for the whole of the *Community* tab rather than only while an offer is up: `MapCommunitySearchControl` draws it while `isBrowsing`, disabled (not withdrawn) above the zoom ceiling, where the list's footer says why — a control that vanished at a zoom level would be reporting policy by absence again. A tap with no offer standing therefore has somewhere to go: `searchVisibleArea()` falls through to `retry()`, which forgets the policy's last query and re-asks about the visible region, because a hiker asking for this list again is a thing the permanent pill lets them say and the thresholds would otherwise refuse as "the same question". While a search is out the glyph becomes a spinner and the pill stops taking taps, and both halves are covered by one flag — `CommunityBrowser.isSearching`, derived from `state` — because the merge asks CloudKit and Overpass side by side and returns when both have answered or failed. Refusing the tap is the point rather than a side effect: `perform` awaits the task it supersedes before starting, so a second tap cannot answer sooner and can only queue another listing pass; `searchVisibleArea()` and `retry()` carry the same guard so a race cannot get past it. The outline fetch that follows an answer is deliberately outside the spinner — the rows and pins are already up by then. A pan still spends nothing, and the pill is now also where a refusal from OpenStreetMap is drawn: a caption under it names the half that is missing and the button stays enabled, because the published hikes are still askable. Both the pill and the pins are UIKit for the reason the camera pill is: a SwiftUI overlay reading `isBrowsing` and `areaPrompt` would put every offer and withdrawal through the root view's body.

**And they are lines, not only points, before anything is imported.** A trail is a line before it is a place, and a marker on a trailhead says nothing about whether the walk behind it climbs the ridge or follows the valley — so `MapCommunityRoutes` draws every hike in the answer, at half strength and underneath the hiker's own route. *Underneath* is a position rather than a level: everything this app draws is at `.aboveLabels`, because the raster tile overlay is opaque (`canReplaceMapContent`) and sits there itself, so a line at `.aboveRoads` is not faint but buried — which is what these were until the level was corrected. The order within the one level is therefore tiles, then the shared lines just above them, then the hiker's own route anchored on the topmost of those. Where the two cross, theirs wins; the tint is the app's rather than `RouteStyle`'s, for the reason the markers' is. The pins stay alongside and that is not caution: a polyline is not an accessibility element and cannot be one, so VoiceOver reaches a shared hike through its marker, and markers declutter where lines cannot. MapKit hit-tests annotations and never overlays, so the tap is this app's own — a recognizer installed in `makeMapView`, `CommunityRouteHitTest` for the geometry, and `Coordinator.communityListing(forTapAt:in:)` as the seam between them, because a `UITapGestureRecognizer`'s state and location are set by the touch system and cannot be driven by a suite. The pick is *nearest within a fingertip* rather than first: two trails sharing a valley floor overlap at any zoom showing both. The measurement is in screen points, deliberately — the tolerance is a distance on the glass, and in map points the same number would mean forty metres at one zoom and four kilometres at another.

**The geometry that makes that affordable is a separate, thinner copy of the route.** `CommunityListing` still carries none: a page is twenty-five of them and twenty-five recorded routes is tens of megabytes for a list the hiker may scroll straight past, which is why the browse path fetched no route at all. `CommunityRouteOutline` is the middle term — the same line thinned by Ramer–Douglas–Peucker to at most 128 points and encoded as a Google polyline, about a kilobyte, so a whole page is about twenty-five. It is a **field** on `CommunityHikeSubmission` where the route is an asset, and that is the whole of why it earns its place: a field can be asked for by itself, so `CommunityTransporting.outlines(for:)` fetches the lot in one `records(for:desiredKeys:)` and nothing else comes with it. It therefore needs **no index** and must not be given one — it is read by a fetch of record IDs taken off published listings, which is the only way that type is ever read, and the absence of any index on it is the control that keeps submissions unenumerable. It is also **not** denormalised onto the listing: that would spend a hand-typed field in the Console on every publication for a round trip nobody is waiting on. Nothing computes a statistic from an outline and nothing imports one — elevation, timestamps, provenance and pause boundaries are all gone and the points have moved by up to the tolerance — and `CommunityRouteOutline.decoded(_:)` is strict to the point of refusing the whole line, because what it reads is text off a public record that a person may have pasted by hand: a truncated paste, an unpaired value or a coordinate off the planet draws nothing at all rather than a route through the Atlantic. The fetch is its own task off `accept(_:answering:about:)`, counted in `requestsInFlight` and deliberately not in `issuedRequests` — one answer is one question however many requests carry it back — and a failure costs the lines and nothing else, because the rows and pins are already up. An absent outline is the ordinary case, not an error: every hike published before the field existed has none, and those keep their pin and draw no line.

**The preview's route is on the map, and the preview's numbers are on the preview.** `CommunityHikeView` used to draw the route itself, as an unscaled sketch with no ground under it, on a screen presented over a real map that was drawing the same trail as a single pin. Both halves have moved. The screen tells `CommunityBrowser` which hike it is about and hands over the full route its own fetch produced (`previewOpened` / `previewLoaded` / `previewClosed`), and `routeLines` draws that one at full strength *instead of* its outline, so the map never carries two versions of one trail. It is drawn even when it is nowhere in the nearby answer, which is the case a hike found by typing its name is in — and `bringPreviewedRouteIntoView` fits the camera to it only when it is not already on screen, so a hiker who opened a hike by tapping its line keeps the context they chose it with and one who opened it from a search is taken to it. The three calls are matched on the listing because SwiftUI tears a replaced screen down *after* its replacement appears, so an unmatched close would blank the new preview's line on the way in. The browser reference the screen holds is written and never read, which is what keeps a screen presented over the map out of the map's redraw path. What replaces the sketch is the hike detail screen's own page, in the hike detail screen's own order: `ElevationChartView`, then `StatSummary`, then the photographs, then `TrailSurfaceSection` and `TrailDifficultySection`, and *Details* last. What somebody deciding whether to keep a stranger's trail compares is their hike against this one, and two layouts would make that comparison work. **The reuse is a constraint on those views rather than a favour to this screen:** each was split in two so the half that draws takes the value it draws and the half that reads a `Hike` stays on the hike's screen — `TrailSurfaceSection` beside `HikeSurfaceSection`, `ElevationPlaceholderView` beside `HikeElevationPlaceholder`, the shape `ElevationChartView` and `HikeElevationChart` already had. That split is also what keeps render isolation: the wrapper is the boundary the write filling a breakdown in invalidates, and folding it back into `HikeDetailView.body` would put `hike.surfaceBreakdown` on the detail screen's own input list. The numbers come from `HikeDetailPreparation.prepare`, one walk of the route producing the profile and the stats together, and the distance is `CommunityImport.routeLength` rather than the listing's typed figure, for the reason the import uses it — `CommunityPreviewPageTests` asserts that against the hike the Add button makes rather than against the function, because agreeing with the function is not the claim. What does *not* cross over is everything that customises a hike somebody owns: no route tint, no line pattern, no auto-follow, no offline tiles, no walk. The chart is drawn in the app's accent, which is what `MapCommunityRoutes` is already drawing the same route in, and its scrub moves the chart's own marker and nothing else — there is no live location to project onto a stranger's trail and no map pin to hand back.

**Surface and difficulty are measured on open and thrown away with the screen.** A shared hike has nowhere to keep them: `Hike.surfaceBreakdown` is a column on a model the preview does not have and must not create to hold a measurement about a trail nobody has imported. So `CommunityHikeView` takes the same `trailGraphProvider` the detail screen does, fires `HikeTrailAnalysis.breakdowns` as the route lands — started rather than awaited, so the Overpass round trip overlaps the walk of the route — and holds the answer in `@State` for the life of the screen. Opened twice is measured twice, and what makes that affordable is `OverpassTrailGraphProvider`'s region cache, shared with the hiker's own hikes and with the recorder. **This is the one network request that screen makes which tiles are refused for, and the asymmetry is deliberate:** tiles mean a provider, the entitlement check, the cache and a download, for ground the map behind is already drawing, whereas the analysis is bounded by `maximumPrefetchRegions`, tied to no account and no API key, cancelled in `onDisappear`, and it answers the question the hiker opened the screen to ask. It is held in its own `analysisTask` and deliberately kept *out* of `discardDownloads`'s wait list — it neither reads from nor writes into the download directory, and making a stranger's photographs wait on a trail graph would couple two unrelated things through one `for` loop. Failure stays invisible exactly as it is on a hike in the library, and a `nil` provider — a preview, or any suite — asks nothing and leaves both sections absent. Still no map of its own on that screen.

**The share sheet's footer is held to what the upload actually carries.** `CommunityShareDisclosure` is a separate type from the view for that reason: the promise and the payload live in different files, and the first version of the screen said "nothing else from this hike" while `CommunityPublisher.share` copied the description and the date and the route carried a timestamp on every point. `CommunityShareDisclosureTests` asserts the wording against a real draft, so a field added to `CommunitySubmissionDraft` that nobody discloses fails a test rather than shipping.

**A suite must never reach the real transport.** There is no sandbox for a public database — a record written from a test run is a record every user can see, and it cannot be taken back. `OpenHikesModel.makeCommunityTransport()` returns `nil` under `AppLaunchEnvironment.isRunningTests`, which is the stricter guard than the `isHostingTests` the Live Activity controller uses, and UI automation is included for exactly this reason. A `nil` transport makes the *Community Hikes* section and the share button *absent* rather than disabled, and `makeCommunityBrowser(transport:blocks:)` withholds the geocoder from the same launches for the same reason. The one way past that guard is `--ui-test-community=<seeded|published|empty|failing>`, which selects `SeededCommunityTransport` — a `#if DEBUG` stand-in with three published hikes in it, no shipping build contains it, and a launch gets one only by naming a scenario. `published` is `seeded` plus a reviewer who has said yes: it is the only scenario whose `publication(of:)` answers with a listing, and therefore the only way automation can reach a hike in the *published* state at all, since `CommunityPublicationCheck` is what writes `Hike.communityListingID` and nothing else does. **That is an exception for automation, not a loosening of the rule:** anything that reaches the real `CloudKitCommunityTransport` from a test is still forbidden, and the `isRunningTests` guard is still what enforces it. Everything below the transport stays the shipping code, which is the point — `CommunityUITests` drives the real browser, the real preview, real JPEGs through the real decode, and the real import. Before it existed the feature had no UI or accessibility coverage at all, because the `nil` removed every control a test could touch.

**Sharing is collection, and the manifest says so.** `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` declares five types, all linked to the user and none used for tracking: precise location, photos or videos, other user content, user ID — the typed name a submission carries, which Apple's definition puts here rather than under Contact Info — and fitness, because every uploaded point carries its timestamp, so the duration and the pace go with the route. `PrivacyManifestTests` pins that set exactly, in both directions: a type quietly dropped is what the file exists to catch, and a type quietly added is a change to what the App Store listing has to answer. The Health export adds nothing to it — it writes to the hiker's own store on their own device — for the same reason iCloud mirroring into their private database is not collection. `docs/privacy/` describes the same thing in the hiker's words. Both were previously able to say the app sends the developer nothing; neither may say that again while this feature exists.

**Reporting is an email, not a record type, and that follows from browsing being account-free.** The public database accepts a write only from an authenticated Apple Account — which is the same rule that makes `CommunityFailure.notSignedIn` a write-only failure — so no permission on any record type can let a signed-out hiker file a report, and a record-backed one would be missing for exactly the hikers the account-free browse flow exists for. `CommunityReport` therefore composes a `mailto:` on the device carrying the reason, the hiker's note, and **both** record names: deleting the `CommunityHike` unlists the hike and deleting the `CommunityHikeSubmission` removes the route and photographs behind it. The URL is built by hand rather than through `URLComponents.queryItems`, because `&` and `=` are legal in a query component and would silently truncate a note that contained one. It is in `CommunityHikeView`'s toolbar menu, alongside *Block*, and reachable in every phase, including a preview whose route never loaded — a title can be the objectionable part. It is deliberately *not* on `CommunityHikeRow`: a row carries a title, a distance and a name, and a report filed from one is about content the hiker has not seen. Nothing claims a report was *sent*, the same distinction the share sheet keeps between sent and published — and `openURL`'s `accepted` supports even less than it looks like it does: it says something opened the URL, not that a draft exists. Mail ships on every iPhone and is registered for the scheme, so a phone with **no account configured** accepts the URL, opens, and offers account setup; a discarded composer lands in the same place. So the handoff screen says *opened in* rather than *waiting in*, and neither outcome is a dead end — the message stays copyable and the form stays reachable from both, since the two cases this app cannot tell apart are exactly the ones where the hiker needs their text back. `CommunityReportTests` asserts what the reviewer receives, since that is the half that cannot be looked at.

**Blocking is device-local, keyed on the creator, and applied where the lists are read.** Guideline 1.2's other half (#249). It is not a report and does not take anything down: it hides one author's hikes for the hiker who blocked them. Three decisions hold it up. *Keyed on `CommunityHike.authorID`* — the creator CloudKit stamps on the submission, denormalised onto the listing at publication so the browse query has it, because `authorName` is free text the hiker types and a list keyed on it would block a string rather than a person and would fail open for anybody deliberately evading it; `CommunityListing.init(record:)` is therefore strict about `authorID` even though it renders nothing, since an unblockable listing is a rejection and a dropped one costs a row and a log line. *Device-local, in `UserDefaults` through `CommunityBlockList`* — browsing works signed out and a public-database write does not, the same rule that made reporting an email, so a CloudKit-backed block would be missing for exactly the hikers the account-free flow exists for; deliberately not in `SyncedSettings` either, so the list does not follow the hiker to a new phone. *Filtered twice, on purpose, and neither is redundant.* On **read**, `CommunityBrowser` keeps `nearbyResults`/`matchingResults` and exposes `nearbyListings`/`matchingListings` through one filter — that is what makes a block reach rows already on screen and an unblock give them back without a request, and what stops the two deliberately separate lists disagreeing about who is hidden. On **request**, both query methods take an `excluding: Set<String>` and the transport applies it before the `limit` is spent, because `limit` is a budget: twenty-five hikes by one blocked author would otherwise draw an empty list with an eligible twenty-sixth behind a cursor nobody follows, and asking the same question again would return the same hidden page forever. `CommunityPageBudget` bounds what that costs — one round trip when nobody is blocked, at most `maxRequests` when a page is eaten — and is a separate testable type for the reason `CommunityQueryPolicy` is: the behaviour is invisible in the result. `CommunityBrowser.refreshAfterBlock()` covers the remaining case, asking again only when a block took the last visible row. The affordance is a menu in `CommunityHikeView`'s toolbar next to *Report*, for the same reason reporting is on the screen showing the content and not on `CommunityHikeRow`; blocking pops the screen, since leaving it up would be the one place still showing what the hiker just hid. `BlockedHikersSection` in Settings names, dates and reverses each entry — a block a hiker can neither see nor undo is its own problem — and is absent rather than empty for anybody who has never blocked anyone.

**The whole community feature is free — publishing and contributing photographs included.** Sharing a hike sat behind the Pro subscription once, on the reasoning that a published hike costs the public database's storage and every later reader's download for as long as it stands, which is the same recurring bill the commercial tile sources put on the developer. What it bought instead was a shared list most of the app's hikers could read and not add to, and a list nobody may contribute to stops being worth reading before the bill ever matters. So there is no entitlement anywhere on the publish path: `CommunityPublisher.share` takes no `entitlement:` parameter, `MapEntitlementState` has no `publishTap`, `CommunityFailure` has no `requiresSubscription`, and the share button on the hike screen opens the form rather than `MapPaywallView`. Do not re-introduce a check there without the decision being made again in the open.

What the gate was never doing is worth keeping written down, because it reads like a safety property and was not one: **a client-side check holds for this app, not against a modified copy of it.** Nothing about payment ever decided what reaches other people's screens — that is the schema above, and only the schema. What is still refused at the funnel is what always was: a hike with no route.

Two consequences reach other files whenever this moves in either direction. `MapPaywallView` must list everything the subscription unlocks and unlock everything it lists, which is what App Review checks a subscription screen against — so a feature that goes behind the subscription adds a row there in the same change, and one that comes out from behind it takes its row away (publishing did). The same sentence is in `OpenHikes.storekit`, `docs/terms/`, the README and App Store Connect's own product description, and all of them have to agree. And `MapEntitlementStore.productID` stays `...pro.maps.monthly` whatever the subscription covers: the identifier is recorded against every past purchase and is the one string here that can never be corrected, which is exactly why the name a customer reads lives in the paywall's title instead.

**A hiker can see that their own hike went live, and cannot send it twice by accident.** Three states, derived in `CommunityPublicationState` from two columns on `Hike` rather than stored as a third that could disagree with them: `notShared`, `awaitingReview` (a `communitySubmissionID` with no `communityListingID`) and `published`. The share button draws one glyph each — `person.2`, `hourglass`, `person.2.fill` — and **all three are live**, because each state has exactly one question worth asking. `notShared` opens the share form. `awaitingReview` was disabled until `CommunityWithdrawal` shipped, on the argument that a hike waiting for review had no action available at all; that argument was wrong by one, because *asking for it back* is an action, and the middle state is now a `Button` that opens the withdrawal form directly. `published` is the state with more than one thing to do, so it is the only `Menu` — *Add Photos to This Trail* and the two ways to ask for something back, never a second copy of the walk; see the paragraph on the fourth photo target below — and the hikes list reaches the withdrawal form from its delete confirmation too, as *Ask for Removal First*, placed above Cancel because it is the way out that keeps the record names. What no glyph does is send a second copy by accident, which is what the disabled state was really protecting: the middle one still never opens the share form.

`CommunityPublicationCheck.refresh` is the only thing that writes `communityListingID`. It asks `CommunityTransporting.publication(of:)` — one record, no cursor, no exclusion set — and only for a hike that has been sent and not yet seen live, so an unshared hike and an already-published one both cost nothing. It is silent on every failure, deliberately: it runs because a screen appeared rather than because anybody asked, so an offline phone goes on showing *waiting for review*, which is what it showed before and is still the most accurate thing anybody can say.

**`awaitingReview` covers a reviewer who declined, and the UI must never say otherwise.** A decline leaves no record, so the absence of a listing is the same absence either way. There are three states and not four; *rejected* would be an observation nothing supports. Publication is also **one-way** here — once a listing is seen it is remembered and never re-checked, so a takedown leaves the column stale, which is the cheap direction to be wrong in against a request per detail-open forever.

This costs **one more Console index**: `CommunityHike.submission` QUERYABLE. It is the only index here that browsing does not need, and it is safe for a reason worth keeping written down — querying it needs a submission's record name, which only its author has since nothing enumerates submissions, and what it returns is a listing that is `_world` read and already discoverable by location and title. The alternative, a status field on the submission for a reviewer to set, would put a writable field on the record type whose unwritability is the entire point of the schema.

Re-sharing an already-published hike **is gone as of 2026-09-16**, and the duplicate warning it needed stays for the states that can still reach the share form. It was the only way to publish an amended route, and it bought that by publishing a second listing of the same walk while the first stayed live — see the paragraph on the fourth photo target below. What replaces it is a removal request followed by a fresh share. That path was **unreachable when it shipped and was closed the same day**, which is the part worth keeping written down: nothing cleared `communitySubmissionID` or `communityListingID`, publication was one-way and never re-checked, so a hike a reviewer took down read as *published* on the device forever — aiming its photographs at a listing that was gone and refusing a re-recording of the same route as `.retreads`. The takedown-then-share replacement had no second half. What closes it is a **deliberate** re-ask rather than a change to the one-way rule: `CommunityPublicationCheck.liveness(of:transport:)` spends one request when the hiker taps *Check Whether It's Still Live*, and `forgetPublication(_:save:)` clears **both** columns once they confirm. Both halves matter. One column is not enough — clearing only the listing leaves the hike reading *waiting for review* about a submission that is gone, and `CommunityPublishingCheck.alreadyShared` fetches on `communitySubmissionID` alone, so the retread refusal would survive. And the confirmation is not politeness: `publication(of:)` is a query and queries are eventually consistent, so a `nil` that arrived a moment early would silently un-publish a live hike and let a second copy be sent, which is the duplicate the whole gate exists to refuse. A `nil` is only unambiguous here *because* a listing was seen once — the same absence in `refresh` still means "nobody has looked yet", and that asymmetry is the one thing to preserve if either is touched. The cost paid is the two record names a removal request quotes, which `forgetPublication` throws away; that is safe only where it is called from, after the listing has been observed gone. `docs/privacy/` and `docs/terms/` describe this flow and have to move with it.

**Photographs can be added to a trail that is already in the list, and that is a second pair of record types rather than an edit to the first.** A hiker who saves a trail — from OpenStreetMap or from somebody's listing — walks it and photographs it used to be *refused*: `CommunityPublishingEligibility` answered `.savedFromOpenStreetMap` or `.savedFromTheCommunity`, and the advice was to record the same walk again and publish a second copy of a line that is already there. What that threw away is the only part of the upload nobody else had. A curated route carries **no photographs at all** (measured: zero `image` tags on 106 relations) and a published hike carries whatever its author happened to take. So three of the four refusals became `.photographsOnly(CommunityPhotoTarget, because: Reason)` — the route stays on the device and the pictures go onto the hike that already exists. `.tooShort` is still a plain refusal because there is nothing to attach to, and `.retreads` is the case that reaches **both** answers: an earlier hike that is *published* is a target, and one still awaiting review is not, because photographs aimed at a submission nobody can open would be invisible until a reviewer said yes and gone for good if they said no. That distinction is why `CommunityPublishingCheck.alreadyShared` returns a `SharedHike` with an optional `listingID` rather than the labelled tuple it used to.

**A hike the hiker published themselves is the fourth target, and the one that fixes a duplicate rather than a refusal.** Until 2026-09-16 a live hike's share button offered *Share Again*, and since nothing can amend a submission that made a **second listing** of the same walk and pointed the device at it — the first stayed live, stayed findable, and became the copy its own author could no longer see. It is gone. The menu now leads with *Add Photos to This Trail*, aimed at that hike's own `communityListingID` through `CommunityPhotoTarget.published(listingID:title:)`, so photographs taken after a walk went up land on the listing that already exists. `CommunityPhotoTarget.isYours` is what the form reads to say *your own hike* rather than crediting a stranger, and it is stored rather than derived because a listing record name looks the same whoever published it and a `nil` author already means three different things. The consequence to state plainly: an amended **route** now has no shortcut at all — it is a takedown request followed by a fresh share, which is what it always had to be. It also means **both pairs of columns on `Hike` can be set at once**, which the model used to say was impossible; a published hike whose author keeps adding pictures is the ordinary case for that.

**A photograph is sent once, and the app now remembers which ones have been.** `HikePhoto.sentToCommunityAt` is stamped by both senders — the hike share and the contribution — and only over the pictures whose files really left this device, since the encode drops a row whose pixels are on the device it was added on and marking that one would cost a hiker a photograph rather than a duplicate. It goes on in the same commit as the record names beside it, and never moves afterwards. The contribution form opens with those struck off (`CommunityPublisher.alreadySentPhotoIDs`, read over `ownPhotos` so the strip and the exclusion are one list), says how many and why, and the strip badges them; a hiker who really wants a second copy puts one back with the same tap that takes any other out. This is the one exception to `CommunitySharePhotoStrip`'s *everything is included to begin with*, and it exists because a second send is a second copy in the same gallery for good. Without it *Add More Photos* re-sent the whole hike.

The target is a **string** — a `CommunityIdentity`, so a record name and `osm:r/<relation>` live in one namespace — and that is what makes the OpenStreetMap half possible at all: a `CKRecord.Reference` can only point at a record, and a relation has none. `CommunityPhotoSubmission` is `_world` read / `_icloud` create / `_creator` read with `GRANT WRITE TO reviewer`, carries **no index at all** like its sibling, and holds the pictures, the pins, the credit, the target and a location for the reviewer's map — no title, no description, no route, none of which is a contributor's to send. `CommunityPhotoContribution` is `_world` read with create and write granted to `reviewer`, and needs **two** queryable fields: `listing` QUERYABLE, so opening a hike can ask which contributions are about it, and `photoSubmission` QUERYABLE, so a contributor's own device can ask whether their upload has been published — without the second, every contributed set reads as *waiting for review* forever, which is exactly what `CommunityHike.submission`'s absence used to do to a shared hike. Plus `publishedAt` SORTABLE so a hike's contributed sets are in the same order on everybody's screen. Both indexes are safe for the reason `CommunityHike.submission`'s is — running it needs an identity that is already public, and what comes back is `_world` read and reachable by anybody who opened the same hike. **The queue stays one query**: `CommunitySubmissionNotice` gained a second reference field, `photoSubmission`, rather than a second notice type, because the queue is asked for by everybody once a launch and almost none of them is a reviewer — a second type would have doubled that standing cost for nobody. `CommunityTransporting.pendingSubmissions()` is therefore `reviewQueue()`, answering a `CommunityReviewBatch` of two arrays; two arrays rather than one array of a sum type, because the two open different screens, publish different record types and are separated again at every use site.

**A contribution does not touch the listing it is about, and the row's photo count is the price.** The `reviewer` role could write `CommunityHike`, and deliberately does not: `CommunityHike.photoCount` goes on meaning *the photographs the hike's own author published*, so it cannot go stale behind a contribution that was later taken down — and a curated route, which has no record at all and never could have one, is not the odd one out. Stated plainly because it is the cost: **contributed photographs are found by opening a hike and not by reading its row.** The alternative was bumping the count for published listings only, which buys a better row for half the list and an asymmetry for the other half, plus reviewer bookkeeping on every takedown.

**Reading them is a second request, made on open and never for a list.** `contributedPhotos(for:excluding:downloadingInto:)` is its own call rather than part of `detail(for:downloadingInto:)`, and three things follow that each earn it: the route and the author's own pictures are not held behind a second query; the blocked set reaches the **download** rather than only the draw, which is where it has to reach for a block to mean anything about a stranger's pictures; and the two sources need no routing, since a curated hike's contributions come from CloudKit exactly as a published one's do. `CommunityHikeView+Contributions.swift` owns it, a failure draws **nothing** — a trail with no contributions and one whose contributions did not arrive look the same, and neither is a thing the hiker can act on — and the answer is thrown away with the screen, the rule `HikeTrailAnalysis` already follows there. It is in `discardDownloads`'s wait list, unlike the analysis beside it, because it is the one that *writes files* into the download directory.

**The gallery is one strip and the index is the contract.** `CommunityHikeDetail.contributions` sits beside the submission's four photo fields and never inside them: those four are what `hasEveryPhoto` is asked about and what `keptPhotos(at:)` rewrites onto the record, so a merge that folded contributions in would hand a reviewer a delete of another person's photograph with nothing anywhere saying so. The merge happens on the way *out*, in `galleryPhotos` and `previewPhotos`, where the author's pictures are numbered first and each contribution follows in publication order — and `CommunityGalleryPhoto.index` is a position in that merged list, because the viewer pages by it, the map's callout opens the page its pin names, and the strip's identifier is built from it. `ownGalleryPhotos` and `ownPreviewPhotos` are what the *review* screen draws, which is the same distinction from the other side. **`CommunityImport` copies the submission's own photographs and not the contributions**, for the same reason the two arrays are apart: saving a stranger's trail saves the walk its author published, and a copy of what other people added would be a snapshot that never grows, never shrinks when one is taken down, and carries no credit into a library with nowhere to show one. Every contributed photograph carries a `CommunityPhotoAttribution`: the two record names, the credit and the author id, together rather than as four optional fields, because a credit with no author id is a photograph nobody can block.

**Guideline 1.2 follows the content rather than the hike.** A contributed photograph breaks the assumption both existing affordances rest on — that a hike's content has one author — so `CommunityPhotoActions` gives the *photograph* its own Report, its own Block and, for a reviewer, its own Take Down, each naming the contribution's two records. Reporting one leaves the trail alone and says so in the body; blocking is keyed on the contributor and pops the gallery rather than the whole screen, because unlike blocking a hike's author the hike itself stays perfectly visible. `CommunityBlockList.block(_:name:at:)` is the overload that takes a bare author id, since there is no listing to unwrap one out of.

**`CommunityPublisher.maximumPhotos` is 36, and it was 12.** The argument for twelve was the bill — the public database's asset quota and every later reader's download — and the bill is a forecast: nothing is published yet, so the quota it bounds is being spent by nobody. It is the **first number to bring back down** if that changes, and the cheapest lever there is: it is read in one place on the way up and quoted rather than restated everywhere else, so lowering it changes what new uploads carry and nothing about what is already published. `docs/privacy/` and `docs/terms/` both quote it in words and have to move with it. Raising it **required a second ceiling**, and the two bound different things: `CloudKitCommunityTransport.maximumContributions` is 20 and bounds the *query*, while `maximumContributedPhotos` is 60 and bounds the *download* — twenty sets of thirty-six is seven hundred assets for one tap on a row. The download budget is spent **before** the fetch, against `CommunityPhotoContribution.photoCount`, which is on the published record precisely so the question can be asked without the assets, and it takes a **prefix** rather than filtering: skipping an over-large set would let a later, smaller one jump ahead of an earlier one and make a hike's gallery depend on what happened to fit. The first set is always taken however large, so a hike whose only contribution is over budget draws it rather than nothing.

**Still missing before this can ship.** Both halves of Guideline 1.2 are built — reporting (#248) and blocking (#249) — and the 24-hour commitment is described in `docs/privacy/`; the App Store listing has to describe them too. The schema half is done and verified in both environments: `CommunityHike.authorID` exists, `CommunityHike.submission` is QUERYABLE — without which every shared hike reads as *waiting for review* forever, however many are published — and `CommunityHikeSubmission` carries no index at all, `routeOutline` included (#272). **The `authorID`-by-hand hazard is gone**: the app reads it off the submission's `creatorUserRecordID` and writes it itself, so a reviewer can no longer forget the one field whose absence publishes an invisible hike. **What is left is not schema, and so no export covers it.** The development container carries `CommunitySubmissionNotice` and the submission type's `GRANT WRITE TO reviewer` as of 2026-09-14, and **production carries both**: it was promoted on 2026-09-15, which this paragraph went on denying for a day afterwards — re-export before believing any sentence in it. And the `reviewer` role's **membership** is a `Users.roles` field on a record, set per environment in the Console: a role that exists in production is not the same thing as an account that can publish there, and promoting the schema does not carry membership across. `cktool`'s management token reads schema and not records, so neither can be checked by an export — only by publishing something and looking. One thing nobody has established: the `Users` type grants `WRITE TO "_creator"`, and `roles` is a field on it. Whether CloudKit special-cases that field server-side decides whether an account can add *itself* to `reviewer`, which is the assumption every grant in this schema rests on. Test it before trusting the role in production. A submission uploaded before `routeOutline` existed simply has no line; nothing has to be backfilled. **The contribution pair is deployed in both environments, as of 2026-09-16.** `CommunityPhotoSubmission`, `CommunityPhotoContribution` and `CommunitySubmissionNotice.photoSubmission` were imported into development that day with `xcrun cktool import-schema` from this machine — export, edit that file, import it back, because the import is declarative and whole-file — and **verified by re-export**, which is the only check there is. The indexes came back exactly as intended and nothing else came with them: `CommunityPhotoContribution` carries `listing` QUERYABLE, `photoSubmission` QUERYABLE and `publishedAt` SORTABLE, and `CommunityPhotoSubmission` carries none at all, `___recordID` included. Import rather than let a first save auto-create them, which is why this was done before anybody published anything: an auto-created type arrives with `GRANT WRITE TO "_creator"` and every field QUERYABLE, SEARCHABLE and SORTABLE, which is both halves of what this schema exists to refuse. `photoSubmission` QUERYABLE is the one that is easy to leave out and impossible to notice — `contribution(of:)` filters on it, and without it every contributor's own screen reads *waiting for review* for good, exactly as `CommunityHike.submission`'s absence once did to a shared hike. **Production was promoted from the Console the same day** — `cktool` still has no promote subcommand, so that step is a button and always will be — and both environments exported byte-identical at that point, `md5 0ebc2f4450be3dba85283442acf7eaaa`. Two things a promote does not settle, and neither is schema. The `reviewer` role's **membership** is a `Users.roles` field on a record, set per environment in the Console, so an account that may publish in development may not in production; `cktool`'s management token reads schema and not records, so no export can check it. **`CD_Hike`'s two missing columns are now deployed in both environments, as of 2026-09-17** (#491). `communityPhotoSubmissionID` and `communityPhotoContributionID` were absent from both for a day — SwiftData creates a mirrored column only when a save carries a non-nil value, and nothing had contributed photographs against a real container yet — which was the four-field `CD_Hike` gap of 2026-09-13 in miniature. **It was closed a different way, and the method is the reusable part: a mirrored `CD_` column can be declared by hand and does not need the device round trip.** Export development, insert the lines, `validate-schema`, `import-schema --environment development`, then promote — no build had to run and no contribution had to be sent. A `String?` on a `@Model` mirrors to `STRING QUERYABLE SEARCHABLE SORTABLE`, which held for eight of eight optional strings already on `Hike`. The cost of the shortcut, stated so it is weighed rather than forgotten: a hand-declared column is an *inferred* shape and not one observed coming out of SwiftData, and a wrong column in production cannot be removed without a reset — so prefer letting a development build set the field once before promoting. Both environments now export byte-identical, `md5 796a197ba5150718ed9077abc9bf7299`, and a full diff of `CD_Hike` against `Hike`'s persisted properties finds no remaining gap. `MirroredCloudKitSchemaTests` will not catch it — it compares two local descriptions and never reads a container, which is the whole reason that gap reached a release once already. Nothing in the photo-contribution work adds to it: `HikePhoto`'s new fields live inside the `CD_photos` blob and need no column at all. **`CD_TrailPoint` is in development and not yet in production, as of 2026-09-21.** The trail maker's marked places are the first record type added since, and the hand-declared route above was used again — export development, insert the block, `validate-schema`, `import-schema --environment development` — then **verified by re-export**, which came back byte-identical to the file that was sent. So the two environments are deliberately apart until the Console promote, which is the only way production moves: development was `md5 831b5dc5c9507a73305ff398507a7e08` and production was `md5 1c90256e479f70124121456c363b45ff`. Note what re-exporting also showed, because it is the standing instruction demonstrating itself again: **both environments read `1c90256e…` before this change, not the `796a197b…` recorded above** — the schema moved at some point after 2026-09-17 and that sentence went on naming a number nobody had re-checked. Re-export before believing any md5 on this page, including these two. The hand-declared caveat applies to `CD_TrailPoint` as it did to `CD_Hike`'s pair: the ten columns are an *inferred* shape rather than one observed coming out of SwiftData, so a development build should save a hike carrying a place — and mirror it without error — before anybody promotes. **As of 2026-09-24 that promote has happened and development has moved again.** Production exports `md5 831b5dc5c9507a73305ff398507a7e08`, development's number above, so `CD_TrailPoint` is in both. Development is `md5 ed35377b48036c8c927e359c049eb394`: production plus the three `CD_TrailPoint` place columns described under *A saved hike's places*, `CD_Hike.CD_routeBorderHex` (`STRING QUERYABLE SEARCHABLE SORTABLE`, the shape `CD_tintHex` has) and `CD_Hike.CD_drawnRouteData` (`BYTES QUERYABLE SORTABLE`, the shape `CD_photos` has), all declared by hand the same way on 2026-09-24 and verified by re-export. All five wait on one Console promote, and all five are inferred shapes, so a development build that saves a place, sets a route border and saves a drawn trail, and mirrors all three without error, comes before it.

## The watch app

`OpenHikesWatch` is a watchOS 26 companion, embedded in the phone app and
built with it. Read this before changing anything under `OpenHikesWatch/`,
`OpenHikes/Watch/` or `OpenHikesShared/Sources/OpenHikesShared/Watch/`.

**One recording has one owner, and the owner is whichever device started it.**
This is the question issue #509 named as the unresolved one. The two
directions are *not* symmetrical, and the difference is the whole answer — so
read both halves before changing either.

**Watch → phone: a recording in progress never crosses.** A watch recording is
the watch's from the first fix to the last: `HikeRecorder` is never told about
it, never enters a phase for it, and has no draft to recover for it. There is
deliberately **no payload for a watch recording in progress**. Streaming one
would make both devices able to answer "is a hike being recorded?", which is
exactly what the recorder is the single authority to prevent — and it would
have to be reconciled across a link that is out of range for most of a walk,
against a durable draft, a crash-recovery path and a trail matcher on one side
and a workout session on the other. A finished walk arriving as a track to
import is not a fourth answer; it is the same thing an imported GPX is, which
is why `WatchWalkImport` follows `HikeImport` down to the off-main write and
the commit before anything is told there is a hike.

**Phone → watch: the recording is mirrored, and the watch drives it.** This
direction is safe for the reason the other is not, and the argument above must
not be read as ruling it out. Going this way there is still exactly **one**
authority, `HikeRecorder`: the watch holds no state for the phone's recording,
reconciles nothing and recovers nothing. It is a fourth *surface* on that one
object — beside the Live Activity, the Control Center toggle and the Siri
phrases — rather than a fourth answer kept beside it. Everything it reads and
every button it presses goes through `HikeIntentCoordinator`, which is what
those other three already go through, so the watch shows exactly what Siri
says and cannot spell the four rules that seam owns a fifth way.
`WatchRecordingMirror` is the whole of it.

Three things about that mirror are decisions rather than mechanics. Its loop
runs **only while the watch app is reachable**, which on iOS means in the
foreground — only while somebody is looking at it, so a paired watch in a
pocket costs nothing. It publishes on a **twenty-second floor**, the Live
Activity's, and sends nothing when no figure a hiker reads has moved; the
*clock* is not sent at all but anchored once and ticked by the watch, which is
the same move the Live Activity makes and is what keeps a quiet walk free. And
a **command takes the message door with a reply handler and has no transfer
fallback**: a fact delivered late is still a fact, but a button delivered late
is a hike that starts ten minutes after the hiker gave up. Out of range, the
watch says so and disables the buttons.

**The precedence rule, and the hole in it.** A phone recording outranks the
watch's own — the same argument the instructions make for a recording
outranking a followed trail, that it is the one that would be *lost* — so the
watch shows the phone's and refuses to start one of its own while it is
running. The reverse is deliberately **not** guarded: the phone is never told
about a watch recording while it runs, so it cannot refuse on that basis. The
guard lives where the information is. A hiker who starts on the phone while
their watch is already recording gets two walks; what they also get is the
phone's recording appearing on the watch's own screen, which is as far as this
design can honestly go without creating the second authority the first half of
this section exists to prevent.

**The link is `WCSession`, and which door a payload goes through is a
decision.** The hiker's library crosses as the *application context*, which is
latest-wins — there is one current answer and the ones in between are
worthless. Everything else crosses as `transferUserInfo`, including the trail
request, which could use the interactive door and does not: what comes back is
tens of kilobytes that has to be a transfer anyway, and `sendMessage` fails
outright the moment a phone goes out of range, which on a walk is most of the
time. `WatchLink` in the shared package is the only place either side encodes
or decodes one of these, and it exposes one pair of functions per
`WatchMessageKind` rather than a generic pair, so a payload cannot be put in an
envelope labelled as something else.

**A recorded walk exists nowhere else, so it is written before it is sent.**
`WatchStore` puts it on a disk queue the moment the recording stops and removes
it only on a `WatchWalkReceipt`. `transferUserInfo` guarantees delivery and
guarantees nothing about how many times, so the import is idempotent on
`HikeLocalState.watchSessionID` — device-local, for the reason `healthWorkoutID`
is — and a walk the phone already has still earns a receipt. Withholding one
would leave the watch offering the same transfer forever.

**The watch matches against the trail itself.** `WatchRouteTracker` projects a
fix onto the one polyline it was handed; it is not `TrailMatcher` and must not
grow toward it. What it does share with the phone are the constants —
`matchThresholdMeters`, `tieBreakToleranceMeters`, `courseAgreementDegrees` and
the continuity window are `RouteProfile`'s figures, and
`WatchFixPolicyParityTests` fails when one of them moves and the other does
not. A hiker looking at a phone and a watch on the same walk must not be told
they are on the trail by one and off it by the other. The out-and-back is
settled by the hiker's **course**, not by continuity: an out-and-back is
symmetric about its turn, so the two candidates are equidistant from the last
match as well as from the hiker, and continuity alone cannot choose.

**The workout session is not about Health.** It is what keeps the process
running with the wrist down; watchOS suspends an ordinary app within seconds,
and `workout-processing` in `WKBackgroundModes` is claimed by starting an
`HKWorkoutSession` and by nothing else. The builder is **discarded** on every
path out of a recording rather than finished, because `HealthKitWorkoutWriter`
on the phone already writes a finished hike to Health and two writers would put
two workouts there for one walk. The one thing the session is read for is the
hiker's heart rate.

**There is no watch test bundle, and that is a constraint rather than an
omission.** A `HKWorkoutSession` cannot be driven by a suite, no CI gate runs a
watch simulator, and a watchOS unit bundle would need a host on a device
nothing here has. So the half worth testing is pushed down into the shared
package, where `swift test` covers it on the macOS host in milliseconds:
`WatchRouteTracker`, `WatchWalkAccumulator`, `WatchFixPolicy` and `WatchLink`
are all value types with suites. What is left in `OpenHikesWatch/` is Core
Location, HealthKit and SwiftUI — frameworks, not decisions — and anything that
becomes a decision belongs on the other side of that line. The phone's half is
covered by `OpenHikesTests/Watch/`.

**Render isolation applies here too, and for a sharper reason.**
`WatchRecordingStats` and `WatchFollowState` are the stable `@Observable`
objects the per-fix figures live on, and only the leaf views showing them read
a property. On a phone the cost of getting this wrong is a frame; on a watch it
is the battery that has to outlast the walk those figures describe.
`WatchRootView` reads nothing at all.

**What the first version deliberately did not do, and what has changed since.**
The first version had no map at all: a rendered basemap is hundreds of
kilobytes per trail across a Bluetooth link for a screen an inch wide, issue
#509 argued it should be figures and a trail-shaped line, and `TrailGlyphView`
drew exactly that. That is no longer where the wrist is. `TrailMapScreen` draws
an Apple `Map` with a `MapPolyline` over it, tuned for hiking — realistic
elevation, muted emphasis, and a hand-picked point-of-interest list — which
costs no basemap transfer because MapKit fetches its own. *Tiles* are still
absent and cannot be otherwise: `MKTileOverlay`, `MKTileOverlayRenderer` and
`MKMapView` are all `API_UNAVAILABLE(watchos)`. `TrailGlyphView` is internal
again, and is now only the iOS widget's fallback. The Smart Stack gets the
phone's Live Activity through its `.small` family (`HikeActivitySmallView`),
with no watch-side code, and Double Tap is the pause/resume button on the
Record screen — never Stop, never Start; `WatchRecordingView`'s header says
why. **The complication is the watch's own recording, and nothing else.**
`OpenHikesWatchWidgets` is a watchOS widget extension embedded in the watch
app (circular, rectangular, corner and inline): idle, it is the app's glyph
and a way in; while the watch records, it is the distance and a clock the
system ticks. The two processes meet only through `WatchGlance`, which
`WatchRecorder` writes into the watch's **own** App Group
(`group.tappium.com.OpenHikes.watch`, never the phone's) through
`WatchGlancePublisher`. What it shows, when a glance is too old to believe
(six hours — a hiker standing still writes nothing and is still recording)
and when a redraw is worth spending (every state change; the distance only
after 250 m *and* five minutes) are `WatchGlanceDisplay` and
`WatchGlanceReloadPolicy` in the shared package, under `swift test`. The
phone's recording is not on it: the Smart Stack already shows that as the
Live Activity's `.small` family. No watch-side
community, photographs, weather or offline maps. Following a trail *without*
recording gets a live position only while the app is on screen, because the
alternative is starting a workout session nobody asked for. And the mirror
carries `LiveRecordingReport`'s figures and no others — no climb, no pace, no
heart rate from the phone's side — because that report is the phone's one
description of a live recording and growing a second for the watch is the
thing this design is built to avoid.

## Settled decisions — do not re-raise

Each of these looks like a finding and has already been investigated. Re-opening one needs new evidence, not a fresh reading of the same code.

**Types that should not become actors.** `TileCache`, whose `Mutex<MutationVersions>` makes bump-then-delete atomic against check-then-write whereas an actor's suspension points reintroduce the interleavings it exists to forbid. `HikePhotoStore`, whose only mutable state is an already-thread-safe `NSCache`, and where an actor would serialise thumbnail decodes that today run in parallel across gallery tiles. `SerialAsyncQueue`, because an actor gives mutual exclusion but explicitly not FIFO ordering across suspensions, and offers no barrier — both of which the "every fix accepted before now is on disk once the queue drains" invariant depends on. `SharedStore`, whose hazard is cross-process and therefore beyond in-process isolation; `options: .atomic` is the right answer and is used on every write. `RecordingStats` and `RecordingTrace`, read synchronously by `MapView.Coordinator` inside `withObservationTracking`, where isolation would put an `await` in the MapKit render path. And `PendingRecordingFixStore.withExclusiveLock`, whose `flock()` is cross-process and cannot be expressed by an actor.

**Older API that is justified, not legacy.** `MKMapView` behind `UIViewRepresentable` rather than SwiftUI `Map`: `Map` re-diffs its content builder on every `@Observable` change, which is the exact cost render isolation exists to avoid, and there is no SwiftUI equivalent for `MKUserTrackingButton` or for the `CachingTileOverlayRenderer` and `DirectionalPolylineRenderer` subclasses. `CLLocationManager` and its delegate rather than `CLLocationUpdate.liveUpdates()`, which stalls after the first fix when the Simulator is driven by `simctl location … start`. The eight remaining GCD uses, each required by an API with no async form or by synchronous blocking work that should not be awaited — this is not a codebase that reached for GCD out of habit, since `Synchronization.Mutex` and `Atomic` appear across 14 files. `UIImagePickerController` for camera capture, whose camera source is not deprecated but is the system camera. The force unwraps of string-literal `URL(string:)` in `MapPurchaseLinks` and `TileAttribution`, wrapped in explicit lint pragmas. The `fatalError` in `OpenHikesModel` for a data store that cannot be created. And the 175 `canImport(UIKit)`/`#if os(iOS)` guards across 52 files, kept as the basis for a later platform target — unbuilt, not supported.

**A store-open failure is reported without attribution, on purpose.** Both the mirrored `Hike` store and the unmirrored `HikeLocalState` store are configurations of one `ModelContainer`, so a corrupt sidecar fails the open exactly as hard as a corrupt primary, and `StorageStartupIssue` carries only `underlyingDescription` — the two arrive as the same string. `loadContainer` catches, falls back to in-memory and raises the alert; the `fatalError` in `loadDefaultContainer` fires only if the in-memory fallback also fails, which is not a user-reachable path. Previous schemas have no supported upgrade path; see *Schema and migration policy*. Attributing an actual corrupt-store failure would need a second store-open on the launch path to produce a message the user cannot act on. `StorageStartupTests.failuresAreIndistinguishable` pins this so it reads as a decision rather than an oversight.

**The iCloud switch takes effect on the next launch, and that is the answer.** `cloudKitDatabase` is fixed when a `ModelConfiguration` is built, so `OpenHikesModel+Composition.swift` reads `SettingsKey.cloudSyncEnabled` once at launch and `CloudSyncCoordinator.pendingRelaunch` puts "Restart to Apply" in the settings row until the next one. Rebuilding the container in place was the alternative and it loses on the case that matters: `HikeRecorder` and `BackgroundTrailTracker` each hold the container they started with, `OpenHikesView` holds a `@State` `Hike` and every `@Query` below it holds more, and `HikeIntentCoordinator` was handed one into `AppDependencyManager` at launch — so a swap mid-session detaches all of them at once, and mid-*recording* it takes the store out from under a live trace and an open journal that only that store can finish. The prompt costs a hiker one relaunch; the swap costs them the walk. `CloudSyncRecordingTests` pins it at exactly that case — a recording crosses the flip untouched and lands whole, and the row is the only thing that changed — so this reads as a decision rather than an oversight. Settings are the half that does *not* wait: `SyncedSettingsMirror` rides on `NSUbiquitousKeyValueStore`, which the coordinator owns outright, and it starts and stops the moment the switch moves. Re-raising this needs a plan for the recording case, not a fresh reading of `ModelConfiguration`.

**Deliberate test seams, not production indirection.** The injectable transports, clocks, defaults, location sources, render boundaries and containers on `OverpassTrailGraphProvider`, `BackgroundTrailTracker`, `OfflineTileDownloader`, `CloudSyncCoordinator`, `LocationManager`, `MapEntitlementStore`, `TrailBasemapRenderer` and `TileSandbox` exist so suites never touch the app's singletons, the network or wall-clock time. That isolation did not go away with test parallelism: the whole bundle runs in one process, so a suite reaching for `TileCache.shared` would still leak into the next one. `TrailBasemapRenderer.Render` is the newest of them and the cautionary one: `MKMapSnapshotter` having no seam was true of the renderer rather than of the framework, and until it was fixed the basemap suite took four live snapshots per pass, asserted nothing about any of them, and cost 570 seconds of `maps.snapshot.timeout` against a 30-minute CI job — green the whole time. A live call fails no `#expect`, so `TrailBasemapRendererTests` carries a `.timeLimit` and a stub that records an issue when a render it forbids is attempted; those two, not an assertion on output, are what keep the boundary shut. The photo domain's ten small types are the same story — every one is under 250 lines with a single responsibility, and several exist because PhotoKit cannot be tested without a protocol seam. No collapse is recommended for either.

**Environment capabilities that are absent, not missing.** `StoreKitTest` cannot be used in this project, and the finding is the constraint rather than the suite. It needs a warnings-as-errors exemption merely to compile — Apple's own `SKTestTransaction.h` declares an `SKPaymentTransactionState` deprecated in iOS 18, and `SWIFT_TREAT_WARNINGS_AS_ERRORS` reaches the Clang module build, so the `.pcm` fails to emit and nothing in the bundle compiles. `OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS = "$(inherited) -Xcc -Wno-error=deprecated-declarations"` on `OpenHikesTests` does fix that, and buys nothing: with the flag applied, `SKTestSession` still does not attach to `storekitd` under `xcodebuild test` on Xcode 26.6 / iOS 26.5. The session constructs, then `storefront` is empty rather than the `USA` in `OpenHikes.storekit`, `Product.products(for:)` returns nothing, `buyProduct` throws `notEntitled`, and storekitd logs the app talking to the *Sandbox* server — because the `.storekit` configuration is synced to the device by the Xcode IDE and not by the command line. App entitlements, stale daemon state and a `<StoreKitConfigurationFileReference>` in the scheme's TestAction were each ruled out by measurement. Separately, `AppStore.sync()` — which `restore()` is built on — never returns in a hosted unit test, observed past ten minutes, so a `restore()` test would hang the bundle rather than fail it. `MapEntitlementStoreLaunchTests`' header carries the whole argument; what *is* reachable is covered through the existing injectable seams.

**Claims investigated and found false.** The widget deep link does not need a `CFBundleURLTypes` registration; the system routes a `widgetURL` straight to the owning app, as `TrailWidgetDeepLink.swift` documents, so the scheme is only a label. A trim cannot delete a tile a concurrent auto-save just promoted: `trimCache` skips claimed names outright, and a tile promoted after the claim snapshot keeps its fetch-time mtime and so sorts last in the oldest-first deletion order. `RouteMotion` really is written by `RecordingPoint.routeCoordinate` and read by nothing but tests — the call sites that appear to read it read `RecordingMotionState` and `RecordingPointFlags.nonPedestrian`, which are different types. Syncing `tileProviderID` does not leave a keyless device with a blank map, because `TileProvider.renderable(id:)` falls back to the keyless default and `SettingsView.providerRow` compares against that effective provider. `Color+Hex` existing in both the app and the shared package is the ordinary cost of a widget target that cannot import the app, and `ColorHexTests` asserts parity between the two. And `PhotoLibraryReader` asking for `.readWrite` is correct rather than over-broad: `.addOnly` cannot read assets, and `.readWrite` is the only level that supports the limited-access flow. The bare `Task {}` calls on `@MainActor` types are not violations of the rule above: every one of them *is* main-actor work — a journal flush timer, a widget-fix merge into a `@MainActor` method, an `Observations` loop that calls `updateEnergyProfile()`, a hop into the `TrailBasemapRenderer` actor, a prefetch that then writes main-actor state — and the flagship example, `HikePhotoImport.discardFiles` reaching `erase()`, is already off-main because `HikePhotoStore.remove` calls `assertOffMainThread`. `Task.detached` would not even be the fix there: strip `@concurrent` from `erase()` and the callee becomes `@MainActor`, so the detached task hops straight back. The escape is `@concurrent` or `nonisolated` on the *callee*, which is what `scheduleLiveMatching` relies on. And `aps-environment = development` in `OpenHikes.entitlements` is correct in the tree: `CODE_SIGN_STYLE` is `Automatic`, so Xcode substitutes `production` on archive, and `development` is what a local build needs to register for push at all.

**Photo pixels stay on the device the photo was added on.** This is about the *private* database and the hiker's own hikes; the community feature publishes re-encoded copies to the *public* database, where the quota is the developer's, and that is not a re-opening of this — see *The community feature*. A `CKAsset`-backed column, a CloudKit record zone this app would own, and a fetch-on-demand path were each weighed against what they would spend, and the answer was no. Photo files are the largest thing this app writes; a walk carries dozens of them; and the private-database quota they would spend is the hiker's own iCloud storage, which is not this app's to enlarge. So `HikePhoto` stays what it is — where and when, a few dozen bytes — and the pixels stay files under `HikePhotoStore`, for the same reason `HikeLocalState` keeps the tile claim set device-local. "Added on" rather than "taken on" is the accurate half of that: `HikePhotoImport` copies a picked library asset into the local store exactly as the camera path does, so the device holding the only copy is the one the photo was *imported* on, which need not be the one that shot it. What follows is a state and not a bug: a second device holds photo rows whose files it will never have, permanently. That state is *said*, which is the part that was missing. `HikePhotoStore.hasImage(for:)` separates it from a file that is here and unreadable, `PhotoUnavailability` carries the two apart, and the strip's tile, the map callout and the viewer each name the one they are looking at — no placeholder that never resolves, no retry offered for a file nothing will send, and no "Remove Photo" pushed at a hiker on the device that is *not* the one with the picture, since that removal would take the row off every device. Re-opening this needs a measurement of what a walk's photos cost a real container, not a fresh reading of `@Attribute(.externalStorage)`.

**ActivityKit's own shape, worked around rather than fought.** `Activity<Attributes>` is a plain **non-Sendable class** whose `update` and `end` are `nonisolated async`, so holding one on a `@MainActor` type and awaiting a method on it is a region-isolation error — `SystemHikeActivityPresenter` boxes it in a `private nonisolated struct Handle: @unchecked Sendable` and crosses through two `nonisolated static` functions. The `nonisolated` on the box is load-bearing: `SWIFT_DEFAULT_ACTOR_ISOLATION = MainActor` would otherwise make the box itself main-actor isolated and the property unable to leave. `ActivityState` gained a `.pending` case in iOS 26, and with warnings as errors a non-exhaustive switch fails the build, so `isLive` names `.pending`, `.active` and `.stale` positively rather than defaulting. And the presenter *adopts* an already-running activity rather than requesting a second, because the system restores activities across a relaunch and a second request would leave two panels for one walk.

**A live recording outranks the selected trail, on every surface, without qualification.** The widget replaces the trail outright rather than showing the recording as a badge or a second line, and the reason is the same one `HikeLiveActivityController` gives for the Lock Screen: the two genuinely overlap — a hiker records their own track along an imported route — and only one of them would be *lost*, because a follow is re-derived from the trail and the next fix while a recording is not. A badge loses twice over: `systemSmall` has room for the live trace or for a trail, not both, and a secondary state is a second thing to keep fresh on a budget the recording feed is already spending. The rule is applied in exactly three places and they must keep agreeing — `TrailWidgetEntry.init`, `HikeLiveActivityController.accepts(_:)`, and `HikeRecordingControlState.init(snapshot:)`. It is total rather than conditional: a *paused* recording owns the widget too, because a lunch stop is still a walk and handing the screen back and then taking it away on the resume is the rule flickering rather than holding. Three questions get asked of one payload and only the first is ownership — *who owns the widget* (a recording exists), *whether it is worth spending on* (`isCapturingFixes`, which is what gates the twenty-minute timeline, the coarse location sample and the Smart Stack's `.fitness(.workoutActive)` relevance), and *what the Control Center button does* (a recording exists). A reader finding those three predicates different is looking at the policy, not at a bug. The takeover is a **projection and nothing else**: nothing on the widget side writes, so the stored trail and its basemaps survive untouched and the hiker's selection is back on the next timeline the moment `clearRecording` runs. That is what makes the budget half affordable — `TrailWidgetReload.requestUnlessRecording()` is the single gate the *trail* feed's redraws go through, because `BackgroundTrailTracker` publishes a live fix every 45 seconds against a recording snapshot `HikeRecorder.sharedSnapshotInterval` rewrites every fifteen minutes, so ungated the feed that has lost the screen spends the reload budget roughly twenty times faster than the one that holds it, on timelines that are byte-identical. The writes stay ungated on purpose; only the redraw waits. Two divergences are deliberate and are not the surfaces disagreeing. A *finished* recording lingers on the Lock Screen for `finishedDismissAfter` while the widget flips back to the trail at once — the panel is showing a result the hiker may not have seen yet, the widget is a glance at what is happening now. And the widget's takeover has **no staleness window**, unlike the panel's `recordingStaleAfter`: a recording payload left behind by a killed launch keeps the widget, keeps the twenty-minute timeline, and keeps sampling a coarse fix into `pending-fixes.json` — which is not a stale surface to be evicted but the recovery path working, since `mergeWidgetFixesAndReloadSession` is what folds those fixes back into the walk on the next launch. Adding an age bound would silently switch off gap filling for exactly the recordings that need it most. Re-raising any of this needs a design for the small family and a reload budget, not a fresh reading of `TrailWidgetEntry`.

**ActivityKit cannot be exercised from a hosted unit test.** Under `xcodebuild test`, `ActivityAuthorizationInfo` reports activities disabled and `Activity.request` throws; nothing makes either say otherwise, so a suite talking to the framework could only assert that nothing happened. Everything worth asserting is policy and sits above the `HikeActivityPresenting` seam, where `StubHikeActivityPresenter` watches it — which is also why `OpenHikesModel.makeLiveActivityController(defaults:)` returns `nil` under `AppLaunchEnvironment.isHostingTests` and the recorder and tracker both take the controller as an optional. UI tests, which run out of process, keep theirs.

**Assumptions that are load-bearing but unobserved.** MapKit is assumed to re-enter `draw` after every `setNeedsDisplay(_ mapRect:)` and to be the only thing that invalidates a tile; the whole overzoom path rests on both, and the redraw loop `CachingTileOverlayRenderer.fetchPath(drawing:maximumZ:isCached:)` closes was reasoned about rather than observed under Instruments, as was the blank sibling that closing it exposed. `@Attribute(.externalStorage)` on `Hike.route` and `Hike.rawRoute` is assumed to be what makes mirroring carry them as a `CKAsset` rather than a record field — documented behaviour that compiles, but nothing here has watched a twenty-thousand-point route cross a real container.

**Two foreground location managers, deliberately.** `LocationManager` and `SystemRecordingLocationSource` each own a `CLLocationManager`, and both receive updates during a recording. Verified rather than assumed: the foreground manager never stops once started, and the recording source asks for `kCLLocationAccuracyBest` with a 10 m filter against the foreground manager's baseline. iOS coalesces same-process location demand to the most demanding request, so this does not imply twice the GPS hardware power; what it duplicates is delegate dispatch and authorization handling, and both deliver through `onMainActor` so it costs no `Task` per fix. The separation is what keeps background semantics — `allowsBackgroundLocationUpdates`, a `CLBackgroundActivitySession`, no automatic pausing — from leaking into ordinary map browsing. Revisit only if a device energy trace shows meaningful CPU overhead, and preserve those background semantics if the two are ever consolidated.

## Documentation

A handful of files with distinct jobs, plus the issue tracker. Keep a fact in
exactly one of them.

- `README.md` is for someone who just found the repository: what the app is, what it needs, how to build and run it, and how it is laid out. Engineering rationale does not belong there.
- `AGENTS.md` is a pointer, not a source: it sends an agent here and repeats only the handful of rules that are tripped over before this file is read. Anything it says has to already be true here.
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md` — this file — holds the durable conventions, commands, architecture rules and settled decisions, including all migration/reset policy and CloudKit schema deployment notes.
- `docs/` is the published GitHub Pages site (`main:/docs`) and nothing else: `privacy/`, `terms/` and `support/`, the three pages the App Store listing links. It is not a documentation folder. `CONTRIBUTING.md` lived there and was served as raw markdown — `.nojekyll` means nothing in `docs/` is rendered — while its actual readers were on github.com; it is at the repository root now, beside `README.md` and `SECURITY.md`. A new prose document belongs at the root; only something the website serves belongs in `docs/`.
- `APP_REVIEW.md` is the text of App Store Connect's *App Review Information → Notes* field, and the only place the background-location justification is written out: Always access is the widget and the Live Activity, opt-in behind Background Trail Tracking, and the `location` background mode is the recorder. It is a claim about the submitted binary rather than prose, so a change to what runs in the background — or to which switch controls it — updates it in the same commit, alongside the purpose string in `OpenHikes/Info.plist` and the toggle's own footer, which have to keep saying the same thing.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `SECURITY.md` are the two files GitHub itself surfaces. `CONTRIBUTING.md` is the short path to a first change and points at this file rather than repeating it; `SECURITY.md` is how to report a vulnerability privately, and owns the reader-facing account of what the public community database grants to whom — the argument for those grants stays in `OpenHikes/Community/Transport/CommunitySchema.swift`.
- `Screenshots/README.md` owns the App Store screenshot set: what each frame has to say, the route and photographs behind them, and why the capture claims a simulator of its own. `Scripts/screenshots.sh` is documented there and nowhere else.
- **Open work lives in GitHub issues, not in a checked-in list.** Missing features, product decisions that are still open, and claims no test can settle are issues on `ZsomborRajki/OpenHikes`. A document does not accumulate a to-do list beside them.

Cite these documents from source comments by *section name*, never by finding number or quoted figure. Numbered citations went stale within a single revision — comments referring to "Finding 1" and "Finding 2" survived the findings being renumbered, and quoted millisecond figures the documents no longer contained.
